cards.back: Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.
A virtual object is an object that does not exist in the real world and can be seen in a virtual world or added to the real world so that it appears to coexist with real objects.

Immersive technology is a technology that produces an experience in which a person perceives an environment through sensory organs as real, so that they cannot distinguish it from their real environment.

An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

Reality-virtuality continuum is a scale whose extremes are a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real, with augmented reality and augmented virtuality as intermediate states between them.

Augmented virtuality is the intermediate state on the reality-virtuality continuum, opposite augmented reality, in which a virtual environment is augmented with real-world images, videos, or live capture appearing in real time.

Metaverse is a broad view of an all-around three-dimensional environment in which people act as in the real world through natural interaction with digital content, reimagining human interaction with the digital world rather than being merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology.
Healthcare is a prominent application domain for virtual reality (VR) and mixed reality (MR), primarily for medical education and training.

Real estate and architecture is a major virtual reality application area in which potential buyers can explore upcoming properties, including properties that do not yet exist, without visiting the place, so they can make informed purchase decisions.

Defense is one of the major current virtual reality (VR) application areas used for training, including simulation of vehicles, soldiers, and combat environments, virtual boot camp and combat training, medical personnel training, and maintenance and assembly technician training.

Gaming and entertainment is an early and current virtual reality (VR) application domain in which immersive gaming products use immersive technologies and players wear headsets or other VR devices to experience immersion.

Education is an emerging application domain for immersive technologies, from primary to tertiary levels, in which appropriate exposure can improve learners' engagement and learning outcomes, although excessive duration may create problems.

The automobile industry is an evolving virtual reality application domain in which companies create immersive experiences of newly launched car models without showroom visits or actual driving to increase customer satisfaction and experience.

Travel and tourism is an emerging application domain for virtual reality, in which virtual tours and virtual tourism let users visit faraway places without physically going there and save money and physical effort.

Digital heritage preservation is the process of using digital media to preserve cultural, educational, scientific, ecological, or other heritage by archiving, digitizing, and using immersive technologies such as virtual reality and augmented reality, allowing virtual exploration of heritage places that cannot be physically visited by large numbers of users or in all parts.

Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.

Heritage tourism is an emerging immersive-technology application for heritage places that cannot be physically visited by large numbers of users or in all parts for preservation reasons, letting users explore each part virtually.

A non-immersive virtual reality system is a limited class of computer application that provides a computer-generated environment in which a user controls characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment. The user is psychologically engaged and remains physically attached to the real world, while the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

Semi-immersive virtual reality system is a type of virtual reality system, positioned between non-immersive and fully immersive systems, that gives the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses while leaving the user free to sense the real world.

Fully immersive virtual reality system is a virtual reality system that completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the virtual world and feels physically present in it.

Three-dimensional virtual environment is a virtual reality environment in which users can move by themselves through a computer screen, VR box, or VR headset, typically without real physical movement.

A virtual shooting game zone is a dedicated fully immersive virtual reality system that detects and translates the user's actual movements, reactions, and even a blink of an eye into actions in a virtual environment while the user cannot sense the real world.
Pokemon Go is an augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

The Gatwick Airport passenger app is a passenger app that used beacons placed at different points in a passenger terminal to tell a passenger their exact location and the direction to move to reach a desired terminal.
Customer-experience application is an augmented reality application that lets a customer preview or virtually try on a product before purchase.

IKEA Place app is an augmented reality customer-experience application that lets a user scan a room and place IKEA objects in a digital image of the room to see how the room would look before purchase.
The Dulux visualizer app is an augmented reality customer-experience application that lets a customer digitally paint walls on a screen and see the effect before deciding whether to buy paint.

Virtual tape measure application is an augmented reality application that can measure the heights and lengths of objects inside or outside a room using a mobile phone, so a physical tape is not needed.

A try-on application is an augmented reality customer-experience application used before purchase that lets a customer virtually try different products on a digital representation of themselves and decide whether to buy.

The Sephora app is an augmented reality customer-experience try-on application before purchase that lets a customer virtually try different cosmetic looks on a digital face and choose the product color that satisfies the customer the most.
The Rolex app is an augmented reality try-on application that lets a customer try different watch models on a digital representation of their hand before purchase.
An augmented reality application is an application that emphasizes augmenting digital content onto the real-world view rather than being immersive.

AccuVein is a handheld augmented reality device that, when pointed at a patient's skin surface, scans and visualizes the internal vein network and can indicate the patient's condition to help decide treatment.

A marker-based augmented reality application is an augmented reality application that uses markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, with the desired digital content appearing at the detected marker's position in the real-world view.

A markerless augmented reality application is an augmented reality application that does not require physical markers and lets users choose where to place virtual objects; it includes location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based types.

A location-based markerless augmented reality application is a type of markerless augmented reality application that relies on a location sensor, such as a global positioning system (GPS) sensor, to detect the user's location with respect to a reference frame, with digital content augmented on the real-world view when the user is at a specific location.

A superimposition-based markerless augmented reality application is a markerless augmented reality application that recognizes one or multiple physical objects using computer vision techniques and superimposes digital content on the real-world scene depending on the recognized objects.

A projection-based markerless augmented reality application is a markerless augmented reality application that uses light projectors to project digital graphics, digital characters, or other digital content onto an object, a surface, or a space.

An outlining-based markerless augmented reality application is a markerless augmented reality application that uses object recognition to recreate the user's immediate surroundings and digitally enhance the view.
A marker is a real-world object or image placed in the environment that a system detects to identify its position or track a user's motion and to place digital content at that position.
Computer vision (CV) is an enabling technology for augmented reality and mixed reality applications that detects, recognizes, and tracks objects in real-world scenes.
A location sensor is a sensor that detects a user's location with respect to a reference frame in location-based markerless augmented reality applications.
A reference frame is a coordinate system in which locations or positions are defined.

A virtual reality system category is a category of virtual reality systems based on the experience or psychological aspect, with non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems as the categories.

An augmented reality system category is a category of augmented reality systems, broadly marker-based or markerless, based primarily on the technology used to develop and deploy them rather than on a psychological aspect.

Marker-based augmented reality is a type of augmented reality system that recognizes a marker image by matching its color, shape, and size, and displays a three-dimensional model in the marker's place.

Markerless augmented reality technique is an augmented reality technique that overcomes the difficulty of maintaining markers in marker-based systems and that relies primarily on computer vision and may rely on other sensors in location-based applications.
A computer vision-based augmented reality application is an augmented reality application that is superimposition-based or outline-based.
A virtual reality application is an immersive application that involves creating a virtual environment, rendering a stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

A virtual reality system is a system that presents a computer-generated artificial environment, provides computer-generated sensory stimuli for an immersive experience, and lets the user's actions partially determine what happens in it.
Virtual is a term that means being in essence or effect but not in fact, that is, something that is there but cannot be attributed to any factual things.

Reality is the state or quality of being real, as something that exists independently of ideas concerning it, or as something that constitutes a real or actual thing as distinguished from something merely apparent.

Sensory experience is a characteristic of a virtual reality system in which the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so that the user immersively experiences an artificial or synthetic environment.
Computer-generated stimuli are stimuli that a virtual reality system provides to a user's sensory organs for an immersive experience of an artificial or synthetic environment.
User action is an interaction by a user with elements in an environment, partially determining what happens in the environment.
Real time is a condition in which interactions are reflected immediately and content loading has minimal latency.

User interaction is a characteristic of a virtual reality system in which the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment.

A computer-aided design system is a system that supports a virtual environment and interaction but does not support an immersive experience, because the user interacts with screen content through a mouse while still seeing the real world around the computer screen.

A video conferencing system is an interactive system that presents a real-world environment in real time through a screen, with the user remaining in the real world and the screen only aiding interaction, so it is not a virtual environment or an immersive experience.
A three-dimensional movie experience is a partly immersive, non-interactive experience that provides a virtual environment, but the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content.

An augmented reality system is a system with four required characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content registered in 3D, that content is experienced through the user's sensory organs, and it supports real-time interaction with that content in the enhanced environment.

A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

Early era is a phase in the historical evolution of virtual reality that existed before modern digital computers were developed and included a few key developments conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.
Formative years are the second phase of the historical evolution of virtual reality, spanning roughly 1950 to 1990.
The modern phase is one of the phases in the historical evolution of virtual reality, spanning roughly from 1990 to 2015.

The current growth phase is the last and continuing phase in the historical evolution of virtual reality, beginning roughly in 2016 when commercial virtual reality headsets made immersive experiences affordable to a large population and spurred growth in the field.
A two-dimensional image is a representation of a scene that can be presented by a display device and that stereoscopic vision can make a user perceive as a three-dimensional object or space.
A display device is a device that uses a pixel grid to render two-dimensional images for an immersive experience, either in front of a user's eyes or in an environment surrounding the user.
Stereoscopic vision is the perception of three-dimensional objects and space from left and right two-dimensional images processed simultaneously, aided by binocular vision.
A stereoscope is a stereoscopic display that creates the illusion of depth in viewed images.
Stereoscopic display is a display that creates the illusion of depth in viewed images.

Sensorama is an immersive virtual reality system that can be considered the first such system under the modern definition of virtual reality and that stimulated all sensory organs with 3D wide vision, stereo sound, smells, wind, and vibrations.
Haptics is a virtual reality output device that lets a user feel vibrations.
A visually coupled system is a system that consists of a head-mounted display.
The Sword of Damocles is a head-mounted display (HMD) that was first demonstrated with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

Head tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality that tracks the head, and it is commonly the most important thing to track and is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears.
A haptic feedback system is a system that uses a force feedback device to let a user feel, through touch, objects shown on a screen while manipulating them.
A force feedback device is an engineered device that provides touch sensation in extended reality, typically as vibrations, by letting users feel objects through touch while manipulating them.
Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED) is the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic, head-tracked head-mounted display with a wide field of view.
A data glove is a hand-worn input device with bend or fingertip sensors that detect hand postures, gestures, or pinch gestures.
CAVE system is an immersive system that renders images in a surrounding setting, making a user feel surrounded by holograms.
World toolkit (WTK) is a software package for higher-level application development in virtual reality.
Virtual reality modeling language (VRML) is a modeling language for virtual reality.
White 5 is a head-mounted display (HMD) with a 150-degree field of view.
Oculus Rift is an inexpensive virtual reality headset that uses the Oculus SDK.
The experimental phase is a phase in the historical evolution of augmented reality (AR) that involved early experimentation defining AR concepts and showing the types of technology required for AR.

Basic research phase is a phase in the historical evolution of augmented reality that followed the experimental phase and involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices.

Tools or applications phase is the phase of the historical evolution of augmented reality from the mid-1990s to 2007 in which early applications were developed or explored, along with exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques, usability, and design theory for augmented reality.

Commercial application phase is the phase of the historical evolution of augmented reality from 2007 to the present, characterized by widespread augmented reality availability and newer applications in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing.

The Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality prototype is the first truly computer-generated augmented reality prototype, combining a cathode ray tube-based optical see-through head-mounted display with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system that registered head movements in three dimensions.
A mechanical tracking system is a tracking system that registers head movements in three dimensions.

The super cockpit program is a major US Air Force research program that produced technologies relevant to augmented reality, and in its super cockpit prototype a pilot wearing a head-mounted display saw computer-generated imagery superimposed over the real-world view in daylight and saw computer-generated imagery replace the real-world view at night or in bad weather.

The super cockpit prototype is an aircraft-cockpit prototype in which a pilot wearing a head-mounted display sees computer-generated imagery superimposed over the real-world view in daylight or replacing it at night or in bad weather.
Tom Caudell is a person often credited with coining the phrase augmented reality (AR).
An augmented reality interaction method is a method for interacting with augmented digital content.
Chameleon is an early handheld or mobile augmented reality (AR) system that allowed a user to move a liquid-crystal display (LCD) over a piece of paper and see virtual content.
NaviCam is a handheld or mobile augmented reality system that superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld and head-mounted displays.
Wearable computing is a research area related to augmented reality that uses head-mounted displays.

Three-dimensional registration is the anchoring of virtual content in augmented reality at a suitable place in the real world so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.
A wearable computer is a carried computer that combines tracking sensors, batteries, display hardware, and input devices to show augmented-reality information in the real world.

An outdoor augmented reality interface is an augmented reality interface that displays information in place in the real world, using tracking to register the augmented reality content in three dimensions.
A wearable augmented reality system is a wearable computer with a headset, a computer carried in a backpack, and different input devices.
Viewpoint tracking is the tracking of a user's viewpoint in augmented reality so that three-dimensional registration of content can happen accurately.
A computer-vision tracking system is a tracking system based on a printed matrix that can enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.
Cyber code system is a computer-vision tracking system based on a printed matrix, used in software to enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

An augmented reality toolkit (ARToolKit) is a low-level, open-source software library for developing augmented reality applications that primarily provides real-time, marker-based tracking of a user’s viewpoint, with only primitive rendering support and no built-in interaction support.
Real-time computer-vision tracking is the tracking of a square marker in real time that can enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.
The Eye of Judgment is a PlayStation 3-based augmented reality (AR) game that was one of the first widely used consumer AR experiences.
ARKit is Apple's augmented reality software development kit (SDK) for augmented reality system development.
Sensory stimuli are computer-provided stimuli that let a user experience an artificial environment through all sensory organs, not only sight and sound.
The technological issue in virtual reality is one of the two major issues in experiencing virtual reality, concerning how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment.
A psychological issue is the human-factor issue of perceiving sensory stimuli suitably in experiencing virtual reality, which technology does not address and which is likely to differ between users.

Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.
Extensive is a quality of immersion that refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to a user, increasing as more sensory organs are stimulated.
Matching is one of the qualities of immersion characterized by congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world.
Surrounding is a quality of immersion in a virtual reality (VR) system that is the extent to which cues are panoramic, such as the extent of visual field of view or auditory source perception.
Vivid is a quality of immersion that describes the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality.
Frame rate is the speed, or temporal resolution, at which display pixels change, and in immersive environments higher frame rates are preferred so that motion is perceived smoothly without jitter.

Interactivity is a quality of immersion that is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.

Plot-informing is a quality of immersion in virtual reality that is greater when the user can better understand, comprehend, or predict the consequences of actions and a scripted story's consistent portrayal, dynamic unfolding, and behavior of the world and its entities.
Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world.

The uncanny valley effect is a phenomenon in human perception in which almost realistic, subtly imperfect artificial or digital human-like figures, objects, or environments evoke unease or eeriness rather than familiarity.
Representational fidelity is the degree to which a virtual reality experience conveys, matches, or exploits familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth.

Interaction fidelity is the degree to which physical actions for a virtual task correspond to physical actions for an equivalent real-world task, exploiting real-world experience, and it ranges from no physical motion to intense, realistic physical actions.

Experiential fidelity is the degree to which a user's personal experience matches the virtual reality creator's intended experience, and it is higher when real-world constraints are placed on virtual navigation, movement, and interaction.
Pose is the position and orientation of a viewer or tracked object.

Pose estimation is the process of determining a viewer's position and orientation relative to a real-world anchor so that virtual content can be registered in augmented reality. It includes a registration phase that determines the pose and a tracking phase that updates the pose as the viewer moves.
Registration phase is the part of pose determination in augmented reality that determines the viewer's pose relative to a real-world anchor when the user starts using the system.

The tracking phase is one of two parts of pose determination in augmented reality that updates the viewer's pose relative to a previously known pose because the user is likely to move, so that virtual and real-world content appear properly mixed.

Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.
Internal factors are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cybersickness.
External factors are the hardware factors and virtual reality content factors that can induce cybersickness.
Motion sickness (MS) is a condition in which the brain receives conflicting signals from various sensory organs, causing symptoms like nausea and dizziness.
Body awareness is the user's ability to attend to and perceive bodily sensations, a physical condition related to cyber sickness.
Latency is the time delay, or time gap, in virtual reality between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.
Latency jitter is the variability in latency in which the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.
Display type is an external hardware factor, the type of display used by the user, that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness.
Field of view (FOV) is an angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is the amount of virtual environment visible.
Visual motion is the movement experienced by a user in a virtual reality environment, and it is a virtual reality content factor that can increase the risk and severity of cybersickness.

Locomotion is the motor component of navigation in a virtual world, the actual movement between two locations, carried out by techniques that let a user move and perceive that the movement has taken place.

Type of content is a VR content factor that affects cybersickness, and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a VR environment induce more cybersickness than neutral or static content.

Visual complexity is an external virtual reality content factor that is positively correlated with cybersickness symptoms, so scenes with more objects of different shapes, sizes, and movements are more likely to induce cybersickness.

Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a physically stationary person in a virtual environment receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration while balance or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict; it is highest when sensed in peripheral stimuli.
Sensory mismatch is a conflict in a virtual environment between the sensory inputs a user receives and the physical movement or the brain's familiar processing, which can cause cybersickness.

Control over motion is an aspect of locomotion in a virtual world, meaning whether and how a user controls movement; greater control increases presence, and its type and extent determine the likelihood of cybersickness.
Transition type is an aspect of locomotion that specifies how a scene changes from one field of view to another and can affect cybersickness.

Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.
Exposure duration is the length of time a user spends in a virtual reality session, including travel and interaction time, and longer duration increases cybersickness.
A measurement technique for cybersickness is a process that relies on an input and generates an output, and it can be manual, automated, machine learning-based, or real-time during the experience.
Questionnaire-based input is a subjective input for measuring cybersickness that generally takes the form of ratings of users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.
Behavioral input is one of the four categories of inputs for measuring cybersickness, and it includes blink rate, head and body movement, the manner of those movements, and postural sway.
Content-based input is a category of inputs for measuring cybersickness that includes optical flow, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity.

A sickness score is a numerical output of cybersickness measurement that quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience and is generally produced by a regression model in machine learning-based evaluation.

The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is a widely used questionnaire for measuring cybersickness in immersive experiences. It contains 16 items in oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales, rated from 0 to 3, with subscale and total sickness scores.

Oculomotor subscale is a subscale of the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) in which participants rate the intensity of individual oculomotor symptoms from 0 to 3, with higher scores denoting more severe symptoms.
The Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire (VRSQ) is a questionnaire specifically designed for virtual reality that is relevant to cyber sickness in extended reality.
Physiological input is an input used to detect cybersickness, because questionnaire-based inputs can be subjective, inaccurate, and not always reliable.
Optical flow is the apparent motion perceived by virtual reality users due to relative motion between the user and the environment.

Manual evaluation is an input-based cybersickness measurement technique that relies entirely on human intervention, typically using a questionnaire distributed, collected, and reviewed by a person to decide the severity, onset, or possibility of cybersickness.

Machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation is an input-based cybersickness measurement technique that uses automated algorithms trained on psychological, physiological, or biometric inputs to automatically determine cybersickness, producing classification labels or a numerical sickness score.

Questionnaire-based assessment is a manual evaluation for cybersickness in which a person distributes a questionnaire, collects feedback, and reviews the responses to decide the severity, onset, or possibility of cybersickness.

A transparent model is a model used for machine learning-based evaluation of cybersickness that provides clear insight into its decision-making process and whose inner workings can be easily understood.
Stepwise regression analysis is a transparent model that is used to measure cybersickness using a variety of physiological signals or physiological inputs.

An interpretable model is a machine learning model used in cybersickness evaluation that reveals how or why its output is generated from its input and provides precise details about that relationship.

Black-box model is a model used in cybersickness evaluation that takes an input and produces an output without revealing how or why that output is generated; it generally provides higher prediction accuracy than transparent and interpretable models but requires large amounts of data and processing power.
Hybrid model is a combination of different machine learning models used to predict or classify cybersickness, designed to provide high accuracy and some transparency.
Electroencephalogram network (EEGNET) is a specialized convolutional neural network for electroencephalography prediction.

cards.front: classification based on the event of measurement
cards.back: Classification based on the event of measurement is a category of cybersickness evaluation technique that distinguishes detection, which uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred, from prediction, which occurs before the experience to determine whether cybersickness will occur.
Detection is a cybersickness evaluation technique that uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred.
Prediction is a cybersickness evaluation technique that occurs before an experience to determine whether cybersickness will occur, enabling mitigation measures before cybersickness occurs.
A classification label is an output of machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation that indicates the likelihood or severity of cybersickness.
Cybersickness mitigation is the use of measures that reduce or eliminate cybersickness or lessen its impact, while balancing that reduction against preserving presence and user experience.

Field of view adjustment is a developer-side strategy that restricts parts of the field of view, reducing peripheral optical flow to mitigate cybersickness, though it can reduce presence and visual-task performance.
Dynamic visual blur is a developer-side technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness that works by obscuring or reducing clarity and has two types: depth-of-field blur and peripheral blur.
A rest frame is a fixed element within a virtual environment that remains stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements, and it is used to reduce cybersickness.

Optical-flow manipulation is a developer-side cybersickness reduction technique that can visually mix optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, use a restricted field of view aligned with optical flow, or reduce perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.
Hardware-level alteration is a developer-side strategy for reducing or eliminating cybersickness by modifying existing hardware to different degrees or by proposing completely new hardware.

Locomotion modification is a developer-side strategy for reducing cybersickness that changes locomotion methods, including teleportation, novel walking, dynamic steering speed, viewpoint snapping, and invisible ramps.
A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

An asymmetric mask is a field of view adjustment strategy, considered an adaptive restrictor, that obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion and only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation, shifting the center of restriction in the direction of the turn.

An adaptive restrictor is a field of view adjustment strategy that adapts based on optical flow by obscuring peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible.

A side restrictor is a field of view adjustment strategy, described as an asymmetric mask, that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn.
A ground visible restrictor is a field of view adjustment strategy that keeps the ground plane visible during movement.
Depth-of-field blur is a type of dynamic visual blur, a technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness, that uses well-known depth cues in human vision.
Independent visual background is a rest frame attached to the head reference frame that remains stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements.
Sparse peripheral display is a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness that expands the periphery of a head-mounted display with a colorful LED matrix.
Phantom legs is a hardware-level alteration that uses additional hardware to apply alternating haptic cues synchronized to users' footsteps and has been found to greatly reduce cybersickness.
Floor vibration is a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness that uses vibration-driven whole-body tactile feedback to match the vibrations of the virtual environment.

cards.front: simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration
cards.back: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration is a hardware-level alteration that has been tried for reducing cybersickness.
A walking vibe system is a system that uses two small vibration motors behind the ears for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience and has been tried for reducing cybersickness.
A modified motion platform is a hardware-level alteration that can be modified to produce short bursts of rotational acceleration matching visual forward acceleration to reduce cybersickness.
Dynamic steering speed is a locomotion modification for reducing cybersickness, and it skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure.
Viewpoint snapping is a locomotion modification for reducing cybersickness that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation.

Maximum duration is the generally safe upper limit for a virtual reality session that is recommended to reduce cybersickness risk for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness, and the limit may vary with device, content, and other factors.
Habituation is the gradual decrease in the intensity of cybersickness after repeated experience in a virtual environment.
A computer is one of the major components of virtual reality (VR) hardware, a device that processes data from input sensors and activates output devices so that a user can perceive the world.

An output device is an XR hardware component that produces output to stimulate a user's sensory organs, not only a visual display; examples include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms, and treadmills.

Sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals, or, in the human body, an organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses; in XR hardware it is a tracking device that tracks a user's movements and extracts information from the real world.

Tracking is the integral XR hardware component that keeps track of physical-world motion, translating user pose, position, and orientation—or real objects—into virtual motion or 3D content registered to a real-world anchor.

A complete view is a view of a virtual reality system that includes the organism, typically the human user, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world, shows tracking from the organism to the VR hardware, stimulation from the VR hardware to the organism, and bidirectional data flows with the surrounding physical world, and the organism cannot be omitted.

Organism is the VR system component, alongside the hardware and surrounding physical world, that is typically the human user; it is always present, cannot be omitted, and is equally important as the hardware, sending tracking data to and receiving stimulation from it, while exchanging data with the world.

Virtual reality hardware is the component of a virtual reality system that receives user input, produces sensory output, and exchanges data with the surrounding physical environment. It consists of displays, sensors, and computers.
Stimulation is the data flow in a virtual reality system from VR hardware to the user (organism), carrying hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses.

Data flow is the bidirectional exchange of data in a virtual reality system that occurs among the user, VR hardware, and surrounding physical world; between the user and hardware, tracking data from the user lets the hardware adjust the stimulation data sent to the user.

Stimulus is a particular input that activates the receptors of a sense organ and is converted into neural impulses. In virtual reality, output devices generate it to affect the user's sense organs. For human senses it can be electromagnetic energy, air pressure waves, tissue distortion, gravity or acceleration, or chemical composition.
Tracking data flow is a data flow in a virtual reality system that uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust hardware-generated stimuli based on those motions.
Surrounding physical environment is the real-world surroundings of a VR user that is part of the VR system because it can affect user behavior through real-world stimuli.
A tracking device is a sensor or input device used in virtual reality hardware to track a user's input and extract information from the real world.
A virtual reality input device is an input device that is broadly either a hand input device, which requires hands to operate, or a non-hand input device, which does not require hands to operate.
Hand input device is a virtual reality input device that requires hands to operate.
A non-hand input device is a virtual reality input device that does not require hands to operate.
World-grounded device is a virtual reality hand input device that is fixed in the real world and does not move.
A non-tracked handheld controller is a virtual reality hand input device that is held in the hand but is not tracked in three-dimensional space, so the system does not know its exact position.
Tracked handheld controller is a virtual reality hand input device that has six degrees of freedom tracking, allowing the system to track its movements.
Hand-worn device is a type of virtual reality hand input device that is worn on the hands, arms, or fingers.

Bare-hand input is a virtual reality hand-input interaction that uses computer vision to track the user's bare hand, detect gestures, and translate them into commands in the virtual environment, without the user needing to wear anything or use any external device.

Break-in presence is discomfort about performing a task appropriately in a virtual world that is caused when untracked hand movements do not produce corresponding changes in virtual hand positions, affecting the perception of presence.
The VIVE controller is a tracked handheld controller that combines a joystick with six degrees of freedom tracking and is mainly used in virtual reality.

A bend-sensing data glove is a data glove with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions, whose processing unit receives continuous raw data from the bend sensors and processes the data to detect hand postures and gestures, providing a large degree of freedom for interaction.
A bend sensor is a sensor in a data glove, placed at a bend position or joint, that provides continuous raw data for detecting hand postures and gestures.

A pinch glove is a data glove in which sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, often including the thumb and index fingertips, and it detects a limited set of pinch gestures for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

The Leap Motion device is an infrared-based bare-hand input device: a hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three infrared LEDs and two wide-angle cameras. Its cameras pick up infrared light reflected from the hands, and software converts the signals into gestures; it can be attached to a head-mounted display to provide hand input.

Hand-tracking sensor is an infrared (IR)-based sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands, the cameras pick it up, and software converts the signals into gestures.
A low-cost head-mounted display is a head-mounted display that does not provide good-quality controllers or controller support.
A cardboard-type device is a low-cost head-mounted display in which a smartphone provides a stereoscopic view and which does not support good-quality controllers or interaction.
Non-hand-based input devices are input devices that capture input from parts of the body other than the hand, including head movement, eye gaze, voice, and body movement.

Head-tracking-based input devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically use head motion for input, and a head-mounted display worn by the user can double as a head tracking device with sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch and infer the input to change the view.
A head tracking device is a non-hand-based input device that typically uses head motion, using sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch to infer the input to change the view.

Eye tracking devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically come integrated with headsets and track where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, helping the system infer what action to take.

The Midas touch problem is an eye tracking-based input problem in which a system cannot differentiate an intentional gaze meant to select an object from a habitual blank gaze, so the system may select an object or perform an action even though the user did not intend to.

Eye tracking is a non-hand-based input technique that tracks a user's gaze point or area, using optical, camera-based or other tracking techniques in systems that may be head-mounted or externally attached, to help a system infer what action to take.
Multimodal input is a form of input that uses other forms of input in addition to eye tracking for interacting with a system.
A treadmill is an output device for virtual reality that provides the sense of walking or running while staying in one place by providing different sorts of input to the feet or legs.
Visual display is a display that is meant to stimulate the visual sense, that is, the eyes. Its three broad types are head-mounted displays (HMDs), world-fixed displays, and regular displays.
Non-hand input technique is a virtual reality input technique that includes head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.

Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method in virtual reality that tracks a user's full-body movement, beyond the head, hands, and eyes. It can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence by showing a fuller representation of the user. Its two broad approaches are motion capture suits and camera-based tracking.
Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays.

A motion capture suit (MOCAP) is a suit for full-body tracking that records the wearer's movements through sensors that capture and transmit raw movement data, which are combined and converted into full-body position and movement.

Camera-based tracking is a full-body tracking approach in which multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement.
The Perception Neuron suit is a motion capture suit that uses straps with inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors on the legs, hands, arms, and head.
A microphone array is a set of microphones that captures sound in a 360-degree environment.

Virtual reality experience is an experience that utilizes human senses, created by virtual reality software driving hardware to generate appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs.

An extended reality engine is the middleware in an extended reality system that is required to support, develop, and render virtual reality experiences by using hardware resources to generate output data.

Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality setup that provides specialized 3D audio to give a sense of where sounds are coming from, using speakers fixed in space or moving with the head. Headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

A motion platform is a virtual reality hardware output device that moves the entire body to produce a sense of physical motion and gravity, conveying a sense of orientation, vibration, acceleration, and jerks; it may be active (controlled by a computer simulation) or passive (controlled by the user).
A sensory output system is a virtual reality output system that stimulates the taste and smell sensory organs, namely the tongue and nose.

World-fixed display is a non-wearable, stationary visual display that renders graphics onto a fixed surface or screen that does not move with the user's head, while the user can move within a physical space.
A regular display is a non-specialized visual display that can be mobile or stationary, is typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality, and is mostly used for augmented reality.
Monoscopic viewing is the use of one small screen in a head-mounted display to place images directly in front of a user's eyes.

A surround screen is a world-fixed display that completely surrounds the user, typically with three to six large screens for visual immersion, is usually driven by one or several powerful graphics engines, and requires elaborate tracking of the user's movements.

A fish tank display is an early world-fixed virtual reality display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube monitor as output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user’s head moves.
A haptic device is a physical object or computer-controlled physical feedback output that activates touch sensation when a user interacts with virtual objects.
Three-dimensional audio is specialized audio that gives a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head.
A haptic rendering system is an output that activates touch sensation and explores touch perception.
Haptic output is a device that activates touch sensation and explores touch perception, categorized as passive or active, tactile or proprioceptive, and self-grounded or world-grounded.
Touch perception is a perception formed when the brain processes neural impulses from somatosensory receptors activated by a hand touching an object.
A passive haptic device is a static real-world physical object that matches the shape of virtual objects and is not controlled by a computer.
An active haptic device is a physical object or physical feedback that is controlled by a computer and provides a sense of touch when interacting with virtual objects.

Tactile haptics are haptic devices that provide touch sensations through the skin, including vibrotactile stimulation using mechanical vibration and electrotactile stimulation using electrodes that pass current through the skin.
Vibrotactile stimulation is a type of tactile haptic that provides touch sensations through the skin using mechanical vibration.
Electrotactile stimulation is a tactile haptic that provides touch sensations through the skin using electrodes that pass current through the skin.

Proprioceptive force-based haptics are haptic outputs that use forces to activate joints or muscles and provide a sense of limb movement and muscular resistance by providing corresponding signals to muscles and joints.
A self-grounded haptic device is a haptic output device that is worn or held by the user and moves with the user.

A world-grounded haptic device is a haptic output that activates touch sensation, is physically attached to the real world, cannot be moved, and can provide the sense of fully solid objects that do not move.
An active motion platform is a motion platform that is controlled by computer simulation.
A passive motion platform is a motion platform that is controlled by the user with no direct computer control.

Omnidirectional treadmill is a treadmill that is common in virtual reality systems and can be active, with computer-controlled mechanically moving parts that create the sensation of walking or moving, or passive, containing no computer-controlled mechanically moving parts and controlled by the user.

An active omnidirectional treadmill is an omnidirectional treadmill, common in virtual reality systems, that has computer-controlled mechanically moving parts that create the sensation of walking or moving.
A passive omnidirectional treadmill is a kind of omnidirectional treadmill that contains no computer-controlled mechanically moving parts and is controlled by the user.

An augmented reality headset is a powerful wearable augmented reality device that presents real-world content with full 3D holograms, is generally larger, more immersive, and has a wider field of view than smart glasses, and typically includes built-in cameras and depth sensors.
Smart glasses are lightweight augmented reality wearable devices that resemble standard eyeglasses and provide heads-up display-type digital content overlays rather than full 3D holograms.

Spatial augmented reality system is an augmented reality system that typically projects digital content onto physical objects in the surrounding environment, so virtual content appears to coexist with real objects and multiple users can interact with it without a display held by the user.

A head-up display (HUD) is an augmented reality display category that projects images onto a transparent surface, usually a screen or visor; ideally the surface is invisible and only the content is visible, although borders or shades may be visible.

An augmented reality contact lens is a very small, emerging wearable display technology, still in the future, that can be placed directly on the eye, is not visible to outsiders, and superimposes digital images or information on the wearer's field of vision.

The Microsoft HoloLens is an augmented reality headset and a see-through display that integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view obtained through special glasses. Interaction takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures.

Google Glass is an augmented reality smart glasses device that presents data in a smartphone-like format, operates hands-free, and supports natural-language voice-command interaction with built-in command detection.

A projection keyboard is a spatial augmented reality system that projects a virtual keyboard onto a flat surface, converting the surface into an interactive keyboard, and it may use infrared sensors to detect finger positions, a more common way to handle key-press interaction.
An interactive projector is a spatial augmented reality system that projects images or interfaces onto any surface, turning that surface into an interactive display.

An augmented reality sandbox is a spatial augmented reality system that uses a projector and a sensor to project a topographic map onto a physical box of sand and update it in real time as users move the sand or gesture.

Handheld augmented reality device is a familiar, accessible device, such as a smartphone or tablet, that uses its own camera to capture a live real-world image, displays it on its screen, overlays digital content on that image, and typically relies on marker-based or markerless augmented reality.

Projection mapping is a software-based application of spatial augmented reality that uses software solutions and standard projectors to create complex projections in three-dimensional space without a surface.
An infrared sensor is an optical sensor that can be deployed to detect or track a pose.

Registration is the step in the tracking process that estimates the initial position and orientation of the sensor or user, so the starting point is known before movement is tracked, and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds. It may be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags, or performed without them using computer vision.

Sense-organ tracking is a tracking category that tracks the position and orientation of the user's sense organs so that a display attached to them is perceived as attached to the surrounding world and the virtual world or user experience is updated. In VR it mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components.
Body-part tracking is a category of tracking in which the user's other body parts are tracked to represent the body in a virtual world, where perfect matching is not required.

Environment tracking is a category of tracking that tracks the surrounding environment not related to the user, and may involve tracking physical objects in the real world. In virtual reality, it can alert users to physical objects not represented in the virtual world; augmenting a virtual world with live capture of the real world is a form of environment tracking.

Live capture is a form of tracking the surrounding environment, generally classified as augmented virtuality, that in telepresence applications brings a large part of the physical world into a virtual world, augmenting it.

Outside-in tracking is a tracking category, based on sensor position, in which the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors; instead, external sensors in the real world provide data to identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation. It is restricted to the specific area where its external sensors are placed.

Inside-out tracking is a tracking type in which the cameras or other sensors needed for tracking are located within the device used for the experience or attached to the user, so no external sensors are required.

An external sensor is a tracking sensor or tracker in the real world, not contained in the user's experience device, that provides data to help a system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation.
Calibration is the step in the tracking process that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.

Integration is a stage of the tracking process that aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment, and computes the current sensor orientation from the initial orientation estimated during registration and calibrated angular velocity samples.

Drift correction is a step in the tracking process that compensates for the difference between estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error. It is usually done by blending values from at least two sensors, such as a gyroscope and camera, to estimate and correct drift.
Estimation error is the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of a user, their sense organs, body parts, or objects in an environment during tracking.

An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a self-contained composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer to measure changes in orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration rather than absolute values.
A gyroscope is an inertial sensor that captures angular velocity. In an inertial measurement unit, it is a main component, and sensor tracking relies mainly on its readings.
An accelerometer is an inertial sensor that captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and in an inertial measurement unit its readings can be used to detect drift errors.
A magnetometer is a sensor that captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes and can be used to detect drift errors in tracking.

Measured angular velocity is the angular velocity value produced by an inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor, which can differ from the actual angular velocity because the measurement is imperfect and is transformed by calibration into a value that is the closest possible match to it.

Measurement error is the difference between measured angular velocity and actual angular velocity in the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, caused by imperfect devices and measurement technique.

A calibration model is a model that assumes a relationship between measured angular velocity and actual angular velocity; one simple model assumes a linear relationship, though other relationships are possible.
Paired samples are pairs of measurements, one from an inertial measurement unit and one from a benchmark sensor, used in calibration to compare measured values with actual values.

A benchmark sensor is an expensive, highly accurate sensor that produces the actual values, very close rather than exact or ideal, used in calibration with measured values from a less accurate sensor.

Linear least squares regression is a classical optimization technique that finds constants for a linear expression by minimizing the sum of the squared differences between the expression and actual values.
Calibrated value is a value that calibration transforms from an inexpensive measured angular velocity into the closest possible match with the actual value, using omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g.

Initial orientation is the starting orientation of a sensor or user, found during registration to set the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds. In a simplifying assumption, it is taken as the headset's facing direction when tracking starts, with the initial alignment set to the forward direction.

Initial alignment is the alignment between the real and virtual worlds set by registration from the initial pose or orientation of the sensor or user; as a simplifying assumption, it is set to the forward direction when the tracking system is turned on.

Current sensor orientation is the sensor orientation at the current time, computed by adding the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples multiplied by the sampling interval over the elapsed samples to the initial orientation estimated during registration.

A calibrated angular velocity sample is an angular velocity sample from a gyroscopic sensor at an instant that indicates a change in orientation equal to the sample multiplied by the sampling interval, and is used to compute the sensor orientation.
Sampling interval is the usually regular, discrete time interval between samples in the sensor data stream, used to multiply angular velocity samples to compute orientation changes.
An angular velocity sample is a sample from a gyroscopic sensor at an instant that indicates a change in orientation equal to its value multiplied by the sampling interval.

Drift-corrected orientation is an orientation resulting from a drift-correction approach that combines, at the same time instant, an orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values and an orientation obtained with a camera, using a gain parameter alpha between 0 and 1 so that the gyroscope orientation is weighted by alpha and the camera orientation by 1 minus alpha.
Gain parameter is a normalized value between 0 and 1 used in a classic drift-correction approach to combine a gyroscope-derived orientation with a camera-derived orientation.

Global positioning system (GPS) is a positional tracking device, particularly useful outdoors, that generally offers low accuracy, particularly indoors, and allows only positional tracking. It is typically used when an approximate position is good enough or as part of a hybrid tracking system, and real time kinematic (RTK) technology can improve its basic accuracy.
Inside-out is a way to obtain input for tracking in which a camera mounted with the user detects external targets and estimates poses from them.

Outside-in is an infrared tracking input method that uses cameras placed in the environment rather than on the tracked object to detect targets attached to the object and determine its pose and position.

Electromagnetic tracking is a tracking technology used in virtual reality and augmented reality that uses stationary transmitters and receivers that move with the head or the user's body and does not require line of sight between transmitter and receiver.

Acoustic tracking is a VR and AR tracking technology that uses ultrasonic signals from stationary transmitters to determine the real-time position of receivers attached to a head-mounted display, requiring line of sight between transmitter and receiver.

An electromechanical tracker is a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links interconnected by joints with sensors, in world-fixed or wearable forms, with wearable forms translating body movement into animated avatar movement in a virtual world.
A kinematic structure is a serial or parallel structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.
A world-fixed tracker is a cumbersome type of electromechanical tracker with a display attached to a mechanically pivoting, tracked setup that has tracking sensors and a counterbalance for stability.
A wearable tracker is an electromechanical tracker that is worn on a person's body and tracks and translates that person's movements into animated avatar movement in a virtual world.

An electromagnetic tracker is a non-contact position measurement device in which a stationary transmitter in the environment generally has three antennas producing three orthogonal magnetic fields, and a receiver attached to a headset derives the head's real-time position relative to a fixed position from the magnetic field direction and resulting AC or DC currents.
A transmitter is a stationary part of a position measurement device that produces a magnetic field or ultrasonic signals for a moving receiver to determine position.

A receiver is a part of electromagnetic or acoustic tracking that is attached to a headset, moves with the head or user's body, and whose real-time position is determined from magnetic fields or ultrasonic signals produced by stationary transmitters.
Line of sight is a line between a transmitter and a receiver, with no obstacle in between.
A vision-based tracker is a tracker that determines poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras.
An optical sensor is a sensor that vision-based trackers use to determine poses, such as position and orientation; its main categories are infrared, visible light, and 3D structure sensors.
A visible light sensor is an optical sensor that can be deployed to detect or track a pose and is used in visible light tracking.

Infrared tracking is a vision-based technique used in virtual reality or augmented reality that detects bright light-emitting or reflecting targets using infrared sensing, is robust to poor ambient lighting, and estimates pose and position either outside looking in or inside looking out.

A target is a light-emitting or light-reflecting part in infrared tracking, bright against its surroundings, attached to a tracked object or placed externally, that cameras detect to estimate pose and position.
Visible light tracking is a tracking technique that uses visible light sensors or optical cameras and is classified into fiducial tracking, natural feature tracking, and model-based tracking.
An optical camera is the most common type of optical sensor used in visible light tracking.
Fiducial tracking is a visible light tracking technique that adds fiducials, artificial landmarks in the environment, to aid registration and tracking of an object.

Natural feature tracking is a visible light tracking technique that registers camera pose in real time by detecting features already present in the natural environment, calculating unique descriptors, and matching scene features with features of the tracked object, using advanced image processing or computer vision.
A fiducial is an artificial landmark in the environment that is added to aid the registration and tracking of an object.
A proportional width ring fiducial is a kind of fiducial used in fiducial tracking, whose appearance changes with distance.
A constant width ring fiducial is a fiducial whose ring width remains constant.
A feature is a unique, already present part of a natural environment, such as a point, corner, or line intersection, that is detected and distinguished by descriptors to estimate camera pose.

A feature descriptor is a unique descriptor calculated for each detected feature in natural feature tracking, used to identify and differentiate it from other features and to match features detected in the scene with features detected in the object to be tracked for camera pose estimation.

Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of a real environment while localizing positions within it, enabling real-time, drift-free tracking of unknown environments.

A map is a way of showing a real or virtual space or place, including objects or points, the user's current position, and routes, and can be updated to support wayfinding, movement, real-time tracking, or forming mental models.

Parallel tracking and mapping (PTAM) is a further optimization of simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). It was specifically designed for augmented reality and allows tracking of the camera and mapping of the environment as separate activities.

Three-dimensional structure tracking is a tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain 3D positions of points in a scene and creates 3D models of structures in the environment to augment the real-world view.

Kinect Fusion is an augmented reality system and an example of 3D structure tracking that uses data from the Kinect's structured light depth sensor to create high-quality 3D models of real objects and environments and uses those models to track the Kinect's pose.

Real time kinematic (RTK) is a technology that can be used with a basic global positioning system sensor to improve detection accuracy by using global positioning system signal carrier waves for measurement.

Motion capture is a technique for digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans, that can be based on any tracking method. It is packaged as wearable suits with tracking sensors that record users' movements, and it can be real-time or non-real-time.
A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that combines two or more basic tracking systems or approaches, typically performing better than single-technology-based tracking.

Software development kit (SDK) is a platform-dependent installable package of software development tools for a specific hardware and operating system combination that provides fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual or augmented reality experiences.
Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.

Middleware is software that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers, and supports the development and rendering of extended reality (XR) experiences.

A matched zone is the safe real-world region in a virtual reality application where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align, so the user's restricted physical movement within it is translated into movement in other parts of the virtual world.

Virtual reality software is software that drives virtual reality or augmented reality hardware so that it generates appropriate stimuli that stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses, and supports developers in creating virtual environments, rendering stereoscopic output views, and incorporating interactions.

A game engine is a software development environment and middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracting hardware for developers to build games or extended reality (XR) experiences. It typically provides rendering, physics, audio, scripting, and low-level platform-specific support.
Environment modeling is the activity of creating the virtual environment in a virtual reality experience.
A high-level description is a description that a virtual reality developer provides to virtual reality software so that the software automatically determines all the low-level details.
A platform is the combination of hardware and an operating system.

Virtual world generator (VWG) is a black-box abstraction of a virtual reality software system that maintains an internal reality that appears real and can use renderers to produce visual, aural, and haptic output synchronized with input.
A black box is an abstraction of a system whose internal operation is not considered.
A head tracker is a low-level input system that estimates a user's head position and orientation.
A renderer is a part of a virtual world generator that extracts information and calculates outputs for a display. It can be visual, aural, or haptic, generating a visual, aural, or haptic display.
Visual renderer is an output renderer that generates a visual display.
Aural renderer is an output renderer that a virtual world generator can use to generate an aural display sensed by the ears.
An aural display is a display generated by an aural renderer and sensed by the ears.
A haptic renderer is an output renderer in a virtual world generator that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin.
Haptic display is a display that is sensed by the skin and generated by a haptic renderer.
Material surface property is a property of a surface in a completely synthetic virtual world that indicates how the surface interacts with light, sound, and forces.
Light is energy that can be described as photons, waves, or rays, can propagate through a vacuum, and the intensity of light reflected from a surface to the eye determines perceived color.

Computer graphics (CG) is the area that addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models. It creates or represents objects, synthesizes them into a scene, allows users to manipulate images on a screen, creates the perception of motion, and renders the scene on a display so humans can perceive it.
Texture mapping is a common computer-graphics operation that maps camera images of a real object onto a synthetic object to create a virtual world.
Matched motion is the maintenance, in virtual reality, of correspondence between a user's motions in the real world and the virtual world.

Obstacle mismatch is a situation, in an immersive virtual reality application that is not carefully implemented, that can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle exists in the matched zone without a corresponding virtual obstacle.
User locomotion is moving oneself in virtual reality (VR) while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched.
Vehicle metaphor is a virtual reality user locomotion technique in which a user's avatar boards a vehicle and operates its controls while the user remains seated.

Graphics processing unit (GPU) is a parallel hardware component of a graphics card, with its own memory, that speeds up the rendering process by exploiting the inherent parallelism of graphics operations.

Physics support is a required key support in a virtual world generator that makes the virtual world appear to behave like the real world, for example by making a dropped ball accelerate due to gravity and replicating how light, sound, or smell propagate.

Collision support is a virtual world generator component that ideally includes collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.
Collision detection is a part of collision support in a virtual world generator that determines whether two or more bodies intersect.
Collision response is the part of collision support in a virtual world generator that determines how bodies should behave after a collision occurs.
Collision is the intersection of two or more bodies in a virtual world, and a collision response determines how the bodies should behave after it occurs.

A networked collaborative virtual reality experience is a collaborative virtual reality experience created over a network, in which a system or server maintains a shared virtual world and must manage user interactions, including collisions, whether users are close or spread around the world.

A collaborative virtual reality experience is a virtual reality experience that may be created over a network in which a shared virtual world is maintained by a system or a server, although such a network experience may not be required everywhere.
Physics is a support in a virtual world that handles an avatar's movement, collision detection, the occurrence of a collision, and the response to it.
OpenSimulator is an open-source system that provides ready-made virtual world generator support for developers building a virtual society of avatars.
Unity3D is a popular game engine that has been adapted to work for virtual reality.
Application software is interactive software that is intended for laypersons and, in a typical VR system, is the highest layer above a game engine.

Physics engine is a component of a game engine that emulates the laws of physics realistically by providing functions to simulate physical forces and collisions acting on various objects within the scene at runtime.

A rendering engine is a component of a game engine that helps generate animated three-dimensional graphics by rendering methods and is typically built on rendering application programming interfaces that provide software abstractions of a graphics processing unit.
An audio engine is a component of a game engine that consists of algorithms related to loading, modifying, and generating sound through a speaker system.

An authoring tool is a tool that lets a developer create software or content by accessing underlying system functionalities, with options for loading, feature-setting, and logic-setting; for augmented reality, it can be standalone or an existing tool extended by a plugin.
