A game engine development environment is a development environment that comprises a game engine plus other components, and it may include the entire authoring tool, which may provide loading options, feature-setting options, and logic-setting options, sometimes through scripting.
Low-level support is a core functionality of game engines that supports platform-specific tasks, including memory management.
Open Graphics Library (OpenGL) is a native graphics library and rendering API that provides software abstractions of a graphics processing unit (GPU) for performing rendering.

Deployment is the development stage in which a built system is made available, either as a native application requiring tailored software development kits or as a web application that allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

Native application deployment is a way of deploying a virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) application that requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, which can be proprietary or open source.
Web application deployment is a type of virtual reality application deployment that allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.
Mobile platform is a deployment platform, typically meaning the operating system plus hardware, such as Android or iOS.

cards.front: Google virtual reality software development kit
cards.back: The Google virtual reality software development kit (Google VR SDK) is an open source virtual reality software development kit used by Google Daydream View or Google Cardboard, although it is no longer very much supported.

A web deployment tool is a tool for web-based deployment, broadly including cloud hosting and rendering, development libraries, complete development and deployment tools, generic development editors, and software development kit support.
A cloud hosting and rendering tool is a web deployment tool that provides only hosting and rendering over a network.
Three.js is a popular library for development support for deployment over the web that is used for rendering and makes WebGL easier.
Wavexr is a popular library for development support for deployment over the web that is built on three.js.

Adobe Flash is a popular authoring tool for creating prototypes with multimedia content for web and desktop platforms, and can be used through augmented reality plugins to prototype desktop and mobile augmented reality experiences.
A skill-based hierarchy is an arrangement of augmented reality software tools into four categories ordered by decreasing programming skill.

Low-level software library or framework is an AR software tool that requires strong programming or coding ability and an understanding of how to call the library functions, with the highest programming-skill requirement among AR software tools.

Rapid prototyping tool is an augmented reality software tool that requires some programming ability and may require design prototyping skills, and is used to visualize an augmented reality idea with simple means before major development and show it to end users or clients, so an unsuitable idea does not require further coding.

A plugin to existing tools is a category of augmented reality (AR) software in which a plugin is added to an existing interactive 2D or 3D content authoring tool that may not support AR content, adding AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration, while relying on that tool for content authoring.

A standalone augmented reality authoring tool is an application that lets users create augmented reality experiences without programming experience, and it is a complete package that includes content authoring and augmented reality support without depending on any other tool.

Flash augmented reality manager is an Adobe Flash framework that combines augmented reality tracking libraries with three-dimensional graphics libraries, primarily for prototyping desktop and mobile augmented reality experiences rather than full-fledged development.

Low-level library and framework is the augmented reality (AR) software category that requires the maximum skill from the developer because it provides access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an AR application.
Marker-based tracking is a form of augmented reality tracking that recognizes a marker and its position.

A framework is a kind of low-level augmented reality software that provides access to core tracking and display functionality for building an application, and that can be created by combining multiple libraries, especially libraries that provide interaction and realistic graphics support.

A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene and supports 3D graphics pipeline operations such as sorting objects by visibility, clipping, and state management, allowing selective manipulation of its nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction.

Point of interest (POI) is a significant spot in a virtual tour, modeled as a graph node or vertex with importance and a maximum waiting time, that need not be a physical object and is visited to inspect or interact with objects.
Visible surface detection is an operation in a 3D graphics pipeline that sorts objects according to visibility.
Clipping is the process in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that discards objects or portions of objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume before projection.
Open Scene Graph (OSG) is an open-source scene graph library that is written in C++, built on top of OpenGL, and supports many plugins for additional functionality.
Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) is an open-source scene graph library that is a successor to Open Scene Graph.

Transformation is a coordinate change that takes a point in an object's local coordinate system to a new point that should ideally be in the world coordinate system, typically by multiplying the point by a matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system.
ART 3 library is a framework that combines tracking and rendering libraries, linking ARToolKit for tracking support with Open Scene Graph for real-time rendering.
Goblin XNA is a framework that combines tracking and rendering libraries, using the ART tag tracking library with the Microsoft XNA game platform.
Metaio SDK is an augmented reality (AR) tracking technology that provides AR tracking in frameworks that combine tracking and rendering libraries.
DroidAR is a mobile-specific augmented reality framework that uses sensors for tracking support, rather than computer vision.

ARToolKit for mobile is a mobile-specific augmented reality framework that is a version of ARToolKit available for mobile platforms and that is integrated with Open Scene Graph (OSG) but developed for mobile.

Flar toolkit is a version of the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit ported to Adobe Flash that lets a user run an AR experience in a web browser by activating a camera, tracking AR markers, and overlaying virtual content onto the tracked image for 3D registering with a few lines of code.

OpenFrameworks is an open-source C++ middleware framework and library that is a non-web-based authoring and rapid prototyping tool for desktop and mobile augmented reality applications, combining multiple libraries to support tracking, rendering, and interaction.
Vuforia is a cross-platform augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) that uses computer vision to recognize and track images and objects in the real world for creating AR applications.

Wikitude augmented reality browser app is a free augmented reality browser application for mobile prototyping that treats the device mainly as a rendering device and retrieves content and user-interface specifications from backend servers.

A non-flash-based browser tool is an augmented reality rapid prototyping browser tool that can avoid third-party browser plugins by letting a developer with mastery of HyperText Markup Language, Web Graphics Library, or similar web component technologies write their own code to create a fast prototype.

Augmented reality software is software for AR content or system development, available in four categories based on required programming skill: low-level libraries and frameworks, standalone authoring tools, rapid prototyping tools, and plugins to existing content authoring tools.
The AR Toolkit for Unity is an AR plugin for Unity that provides marker-based tracking, image-based or computer-vision-based tracking, and AR visualization support.

Wikitude Studio is a standalone, web-based augmented reality authoring tool that allowed users to create rich mobile augmented reality content and deploy it either to an augmented reality browser app or as a custom mobile app, including 3D models and animations registered to the real world.

Interaction is the activity that takes place between a user and a system, often by manipulating an image or parts of it with input devices. In immersive environments it is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and system control.
Human factors is the system-design consideration that requires knowing users’ differing expectations, needs, skills, and how they perceive stimuli, so that suitable input and output can be designed.

Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

Disappearing technology is the statement that the most profound technologies are those that disappear from the user's perception, so that the user feels they are dealing with any other item rather than a specialized technological item.
The earliest computer is a computer that occupied a huge room with many wires, whose programming involved reconnecting the wires, and that was accessible only to a very few select people.

Internet of Things (IoT) is a current stage in the development of computer systems in which users are surrounded by multiple connected computers that can communicate with each other without the user separately operating them, moving toward making technology disappear from the user's point of view.
A lay person is a user of an interactive system who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works.

A user-centric approach is the process of designing computer systems in which users' needs and expectations are taken care of by considering user characteristics, starting with understanding those characteristics, needs, and expectations, then designing the system on that basis.
Layout is a design that organizes interface elements on a screen or interface to meet user expectations.

An interface is the way a system interfaces with users, its environment, and other systems, letting users provide input, see outcomes, and act on outcomes; on a computer screen it is the whole content seen there.

Human-computer interaction (HCI) is the discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use and with studying the major phenomena surrounding interactive computing systems; its core concern is incorporating humans into the design by first understanding users and then incorporating user characteristics into the design.
ACM SIGCHI is the official body that deals with human-computer interaction (HCI) and provides the definition of HCI.
Input device is XR hardware that captures or tracks a user's input, actions, or positions and sends that data to an XR system for processing.

Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

An extended reality system is an interactive system that comprises hardware, an XR engine as middleware, and the application layer, in which input devices track the user's actions and positions, send them as input data, the data is processed to render an environment, and output devices stimulate the user's senses.

cards.front: novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization
cards.back: Novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization is a broad three-class classification of interactive-system users that distinguishes first-time, occasional, and regular long-term users, with expert users meaning efficient system users rather than technology experts, and provides a starting point for understanding likely user behavior and making design decisions instead of always starting with empirical or field studies.
A novice user is an interactive-system user who uses the system for the first time.
An intermittent user is an interactive-system user who uses the system occasionally.
Expert user is an interactive-system user who uses the system regularly over a long period and can use it efficiently, rather than being a technology expert.

User-centered design (UCD) is a design approach in which users are actively or passively involved in the overall design lifecycle, and the design is based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, ideally from the users' point of view rather than the programmer's convenience, to build a usable application.

The International Standards Organization 9241-210-2009 standard is a standard that defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.
Effectiveness is a measure of usability that indicates whether a user can do what they want to do.
Efficiency is one of the measures of usability that shows how fast a user can do what they want to do.
Satisfaction is a usability measure that indicates how satisfied a user is when using a system.
Context of use is the specific usage scenario or work setting in which users perform tasks with a product, with respect to which its usability is defined.
Cooperative design is a term that refers to taking users into the design process.
Participatory design is a design term that refers to taking users into the design process.
Contextual design is a term that is more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refers to taking users into the design process.
Human-centered design is a term that refers to taking users into the design process.
User-centric software design is the design of usable systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons.
Extended reality software is software that creates a relationship between a user and a virtual environment.
Input data is the data of a user's tracked actions and positions that input devices send in an XR system.
Output data is data that the XR engine generates in an XR system and that output devices use to stimulate the user's senses.
A sensory organ is hardware of sensing in the human body that contains receptors that receive stimuli and is designed to perceive the real world rather than a virtual world.

Human perception is formed by the combination of physiology and experience stored in long-term memory; understanding it is needed to design better virtual reality systems or to identify and resolve their flaws.
Output is the stimuli that an XR system generates so that the user can sense, understand, and perceive them, in order to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality.
Sense is one of six human senses—vision, auditory, touch, balance, taste, or smell—each classified by a stimulus, receptors, and a sense organ in which the receptors receive the stimulus.
Interaction design is the activity of designing user input in an XR system from the user's point of view to make the user's interaction easy, effective, and seamless.

Perceptual design is the user-centered design and modeling of output stimuli in an extended reality system so that generated stimuli match the user's perception and are appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived.
Smell is a human chemical sense in which chemoreceptors in the nasal passage work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations.

Illusion of reality is the best possible sense of reality, not actual reality, created by an XR system's interaction and perceptual stimuli to enhance presence, and creating it is especially crucial in virtual reality.
Artificial stimulation is the sensory signals that virtual reality generally provides to the brain, inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

Non-adaptation is the body's inability to adapt to generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation, which can cause increased fatigue or headaches and may lead to cyber sickness, such as dizziness, nausea, or other symptoms.
Perceptual psychology is the science that explains how the brain converts sensory stimulation received by sensors from the real world into perceived phenomena.

A receptor is a bodily sensor that is part of a sense organ, targets particular stimuli, and is activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives. Types include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, mechanoreceptors, and thermoreceptors.
Visual sense is a human sense that has electromagnetic energy as its stimulus, photoreceptors as its receptors, and the eye as its sense organ.
Photoreceptor is a bodily sensor in the eye's retina that is activated only by visible light and converts visible light into neural pulses for visual perception.
Auditory sense is a human sense that responds to air pressure waves via mechanoreceptors in the ear.
Mechanoreceptor is a type of receptor that senses motion, vibration, or gravitational force and is involved in the auditory, touch, and balance senses.
Touch is a human sense that detects tissue distortion with mechanoreceptors and temperature changes with thermoreceptors in the skin and muscles.
A thermoreceptor is a receptor involved in the sense of touch that detects changes in temperature.
Skin is a sense organ for touch that has epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis layers, with touch receptors embedded in the epidermis and dermis.
Balance sense is one of the six human senses that involves mechanoreceptors for gravity or acceleration and helps a person know which way the head is oriented, including the upward direction.
Taste is a human chemical sense that uses chemoreceptors in the mouth, particularly on the tongue, to provide signals based on the chemical composition of matter.

A chemoreceptor is a type of receptor that provides signals based on the chemical composition of matter through chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations; not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli.
Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon in which the receptors in a sense organ, as bodily sensors, target particular stimuli and are activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.
Sense organ is a bodily organ whose receptors target particular stimuli and are activated only when a particular type of stimulus arrives, converting the stimulus into neural impulses for perception.

Perception is the abstract level of the perceptual process that follows sensing, in which the brain interprets a stimulus by combining sensory signals with long-term memory and learned experience, not by sensory input alone.

Perceptual process is a process that proceeds from sensing, the lowest level, to perception, a very abstract level, and perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.
Sensing is the lowest level of the perceptual process, in which sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.
Neuron is a part of the brain that aggregates information from other neurons through dendrites, processes it in its cell body, and transmits it to other neurons through axons across synapses.
The cerebral cortex is a large, heavily folded sheet of neurons, the part of the brain responsible for perception and other functions such as attention, memory, language, and consciousness.
A cell body is the part of a neuron that processes input carried toward it by dendrites and transmits that processing to other neurons through axons.

Dendrite is a part of a neuron that carries neural impulses toward the cell body, through which the neuron aggregates information from other neurons. It receives signals from a paired axon across a gap called a synapse, without physical connection.
An axon is a part of a neuron that carries neural impulses away from the cell body to other neurons, with electrical or chemical signals crossing a synapse to a dendrite of the next neuron.

Neural interconnection is the network of connections among neurons, which can be thought of as a directed graph in which cell bodies are nodes that process input, dendrites are input edges, and axons are output edges.
A directed graph is a network of nodes connected by input edges toward the nodes and output edges away from the nodes.
A neural network is an interconnection of neurons, thought of as a directed graph, that carries neural impulses from sense organs to the brain.
Input edge is a dendrite in a directed graph of neurons that carries neural impulses toward a cell body.
An output edge is an edge in a directed graph of neuron interconnection that carries neural impulses away from a cell body, corresponding to an axon.
A synapse is the gap between an axon of one neuron and a dendrite of the next neuron, across which electrical or chemical signals are passed for communication between neurons.

Hierarchical processing is the neural processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex, where signals are combined at successive levels into higher-level information that enables increasingly complex patterns to be detected.

Staged aggregation is a process in hierarchical processing in which signals from numerous receptors of different types are combined at successive levels by neurons until the cerebral cortex is reached, with each level producing higher-level information rather than lower-level information.

Interpretation of a stimulus is the result produced, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and it depends on the interpreter's long-term experience.
Perceptual processing is the outcome of hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience.

Proprioception is a sense of the human somatosensory system that gives conscious awareness of the pose and movement of each movable body part relative to other body parts, and of the muscular effort involved in moving them.
Muscular effort is the amount of effort involved in, or required to, moving body parts.
The motor cortex is a part of the brain that controls body motion and sends efference copies to other parts of the brain to communicate what motions have been executed.

Efference copy is a signal that the motor cortex sends to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to communicate executed motions so relative positions of body parts and muscular effort required to move them can be understood.
Virtual reality headset is a wearable display that places a screen close to the eyes and uses a lens to focus the screen's light on the retina, making the screen appear as a virtual image.

The human eye is the sense organ for vision that contains a cornea, iris, pupil, and natural lens and focuses visible light on the retina, where photoreceptors convert it into neural pulses sent to the brain.
Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light to violet light, that can excite the cones in the eye and produce color perception.
Retina is the non-planar image surface at the back of the eye where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain by optic nerve fibers.
A lens is an engineered part of a virtual reality headset or a natural part of the human eye that guides and refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.

Photon view is one of the views of light that describes light as a large number of photons, tiny energy particles moving through space at a very high speed, often called the speed of light, and is helpful for understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.
Wave view is one of three views of light that describes light as waves, ripples through space, and is helpful for explaining the spectrum of color.
The ray view is a view of light that describes it as rays, which are trajectories or paths assumed to be traces of the motion of a single hypothetical photon.

A photon is a tiny energy particle that moves through space at a very high speed, often called the speed of light, and is helpful for understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.
The speed of light is the very high speed at which photons, tiny energy particles, move through space.
Wave is a ripple through space that helps explain the spectrum of color rather than explaining color in terms of light as particles.
A ray is a trajectory or path in the ray view of light that is assumed to be the trace of the motion of a single hypothetical photon.
Transmission is a possible interaction when light rays strike a material surface, in which some of the rays pass through the material and come out of it.

Absorption is one of the possible interactions of light rays with a material surface in which some of the light rays that strike the surface are absorbed by the material and terminate inside it, so they do not propagate further outside it.
Reflection is one of the possible interactions between a light ray and a material surface, in which the light ray is reflected from the surface without entering or penetrating it.
Color perception is photopic vision, which visible light waves produce by exciting the cones in the eye and which gives a sense of color.
Ambient light is light that falls on a surface after being reflected from surrounding surfaces.
The cornea is a refracting medium in the human eye that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, helping focus incoming light onto the retina.

The pupil is the part of the human eye between the cornea and the lens through which incident light passes, and it is dilated or constricted by the iris to control the amount of light entering the eye.
Aqueous humor is an internal semi-liquid medium of the human eye that lies between the cornea and the pupil and through which light passes before reaching the retina.
Vitreous humor is an internal semi-liquid medium in the human eye, between the lens and the retina, through which light passes before reaching the retina.
Iris is a part of the human eye that controls the amount of light entering it by dilating or constricting the pupil, typically dilating it in dark surroundings and constricting it in bright light.
An optic nerve fiber is a neuron in the retina that carries the visual signal to the brain.

A rod is a type of photoreceptor in the human eye, more numerous in the peripheral retina, that is used for peripheral scotopic vision, and multiple such photoreceptors can share one optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light.

Cone is a photoreceptor in the human eye, mainly located in the fovea, the central region of the retina, that is used for photopic vision, in which color is perceived, and is served by approximately one optic nerve fiber, which aids image acuity.
Fovea is the small central region of the retina that has the greatest concentration of photoreceptors, particularly cones.
Photopic vision is a form of vision accomplished only with cones, in which visible light can excite those cones and color is perceived; it is more related to direct or central vision.
Central vision is one of the two types of human vision that requires the eyes to be focused and pointed straight at an object to perceive a sharp color image.
Scotopic vision is a type of vision, accomplished only with rods, that is more related to peripheral vision and perceives weak lights as grays, with poor color perception.

Peripheral vision is a type of human vision supported by the peripheral region of the retina, where photoreceptor density is lower, with lower rod density and very low cone density, and it detects movement better than central vision but does not provide effective color perception.
Violet light is visible light that has a frequency of 7.5 × 10^14 hertz and a wavelength of 400 nanometers.
Blind spot is a region of the retina with no photoreceptors, so light or visual stimuli falling there produce no perception.

Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processing the left image and the right eye processing the right image, with a common part seen by both eyes and some parts seen by only one eye.
The natural lens is the convex lens inside the human eye with variable focal depth that works with the cornea to focus light on the retina.
A lens setup is an artificially created setup in which light passes through air after the lens and which has a focal plane.
A view frustum is the region visible to the human eye.

Binocular vision is a form of vision in which both eyes see the same image over a common region, and their left and right two-dimensional images are processed to enhance depth perception and produce a three-dimensional view.
A three-dimensional view is a view of objects that is generated by the simultaneous processing of left and right two-dimensional images.
Translational movement is a type of three-dimensional movement in a virtual world that is used for navigating in that world.
Rotational movement is a type of movement in a 3D virtual world that is primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

Degree of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space; in 3D space, an object can have six degrees of freedom: three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes, and three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch.

Six degrees of freedom is the total of six freedoms an object can have in three-dimensional space, consisting of three rotational freedoms called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational freedoms along the x, y, and z axes.
Rotational degree of freedom is a degree of freedom of an object in three-dimensional space that is rotational rather than translational, and is one of yaw, roll, or pitch.
Translational degree of freedom is a degree of freedom of an object in three-dimensional space, along one of the x, y, or z axes.
Spatial resolution is the needed number of pixels per square area that a display must have to match the performance of the human visual sense.
Intensity resolution is the number of producible intensity values in a display, determined by how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality.
Intensity range is the minimum and maximum of the producible intensity values that a display can process to match human visual sense without compromising perceptual quality.

Temporal resolution is the frame rate, or speed at which display pixels change, that in a VR headset must be much higher than ordinary television or movie standards to allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

Aliasing is distortion that may occur when scan conversion renders pixels close to, rather than exactly on, points of an original shape, making lines, especially diagonals, appear jagged or staircase-shaped.

The screen door effect is an effect in which an image appears to have a screen on top of it, commonly noticed in images produced by liquid crystal display projectors and can occur in virtual reality headsets.

A retina display is a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), although for head-mounted or other wearable displays close to the eye the traditional 326 ppi criterion is not very suitable and the required ppi is probably seven to eight times higher.
Pixels per linear inch (ppi) is a display-resolution measure used to state a minimum resolution criterion, with a traditional value suitable for distant displays but not for close displays.

A retina display criterion is a display-resolution criterion requiring a minimum of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), suitable for displays at a distance from the eye but not very suitable for close-to-eye head-mounted or wearable displays, which may need seven to eight times higher resolution.
A wearable display is a virtual reality headset or augmented reality head-mounted display in which a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye.
A magnifying lens is a lens used in augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays, virtual reality (VR) headsets, or other wearable displays to bring a display close to the eye.

Sound is a vibration that requires a medium, usually air, to propagate as pressure variations from compression to rarefaction, and it is perceived at the human eardrum as an auditory experience. It is represented as a sound wave characterized by frequency, amplitude, and phase.
Frequency is a property of a sound wave, measured in hertz (Hz), that is the number of changes from one maximum to another maximum per second.
An audio component is a component of a virtual reality system that combines sound with vision to enhance the immersive experience, make the virtual environment believable, and increase presence.
Audio recording is the recording of sound, speech, or non-speech sound.
Audio reproduction is output generation that can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing.
Cave-like virtual reality version is a virtual reality version that is a surround environment surrounded by display devices.
Headset virtual reality version is a wearable display version of virtual reality.
Believable is the degree to which a virtual experience is closer to reality and everyday experience.

Pressure variation is a change in pressure over time that causes sound propagation through a medium, created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, ranges from compression to rarefaction extremes, and is converted into an auditory experience at the human eardrum.
Compression extreme is the end of the pressure variations in sound propagation through a medium where pressure is extremely high.
Decompression extreme is the very low pressure extreme of the pressure variations that cause sound to propagate through a medium.
A sound wave is a plot of air pressure variation against time, in which pressure varies from one extreme to another like a sinusoidal wave.
Human audible frequency range is the range of frequencies, from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, that are audible to the human ear, and is a limitation of human physiology.
Amplitude is a property of a sound wave that is the maximum displacement from the wave's mean or rest position, measured in decibels relative to the minimum sound detectable by humans at 1000 Hz.
Phase is a property of a sound wave that is the start position of a cycle of the wave, which can begin from 0 to 360 degrees and is measured in degrees.
The human hearing system is a three-part system that contains the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.

The outer ear is the part of the human hearing system that receives a sound wave in its receiver part and forces it to propagate through the outer-ear canal, which boosts sound pressure for a range of frequencies, while its complex folds attenuate high-frequency sound waves.
Middle ear is a part of the human hearing system that is an air-filled chamber in which sound vibrations from the tympanic membrane are transferred to the malleus, incus, and stapes.
The inner ear is one of the three parts of the human hearing system, and it houses the cochlea, the sense organ for hearing.

The receiver part is a part of the outer ear that receives a sound wave and forces it to propagate through the outer-ear canal; its complex folds, together with those in the canal, attenuate high-frequency sound waves.

The outer-ear canal is a canal in the outer ear through which sound waves pass, working as an amplifier that boosts sound pressure for a range of frequencies, while its complex folds attenuate high-frequency waves.
An amplifier is a part that boosts the sound pressure of a sound wave for a range of frequencies.
An ossicle is one of the three parts in an air-filled chamber of the middle ear, the malleus, incus, and stapes, to which vibration from the tympanic membrane is transferred.
The cochlea is the sense organ for hearing in the inner ear that is connected to nerves and converts sound energy into neural impulses transmitted to the brain through the neural network.
Pitch is the frequency of a sound wave, as referred to in pitch perception.

Sound perception is the perception of sounds at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—where social helps individuals carry out social interactions, warning provides an alert or warning, and primitive is the intuitive perception of mostly ignored background noises that may not lead to meaningful action, and these levels together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.
Social-level sound perception is a level of sound perception, one of three, that helps an individual carry out social interactions with other individuals.
Warning-level sound perception is the level of sound perception that provides an alert or warning about something.

Primitive-level sound perception is a level of sound perception involving the intuitive perception of naive sounds, such as background noises, that people mostly ignore and that may not lead to any meaningful action.
Psychophysics is the scientific study that examines perceptual phenomena produced by physical stimuli.
Psychoacoustics is a more specific area of psychophysics that scientifically studies the perceptual phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli or sound.
Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that relates perceived magnitude P to physical stimulus magnitude M by P = C M^x, where x is an exponent and C a constant depending on units.
Perceived magnitude is the magnitude of a physical stimulus as perceived, represented by P in Stevens' power law.
Exponent is the value in Stevens' power law that relates the actual magnitude of a physical stimulus to its perceived magnitude.
Just noticeable difference (JND) is the amount of change in a stimulus required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.

Weber's law is a law from psychophysics that states the just noticeable difference, the noticeable change in a stimulus's magnitude or intensity, is a constant fraction of the stimulus's magnitude or intensity.
Sound localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it.
Minimum audible angle (MAA) is the minimum angular variation in the direction of a sound source that a human listener can detect, depending on the sound's frequency and direction.
Spherical coordinate system is a coordinate system with the listener's head as the origin, used to represent a sound source location using azimuth, elevation, and radius.

Azimuth is the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction in a spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location, ranging from -180 to 180 degrees.

Elevation is a parameter in the spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location, and it is the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees.
Radius is a parameter in a spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location that specifies the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

A sound localization cue is a cue that is either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears, and can indicate the direction from which a sound is coming or be used to locate the source.
A monaural sound localization cue is a sound localization cue involving a single ear.
A binaural sound localization cue is a sound localization cue that involves both ears.

Interaural level difference (ILD) is a binaural sound localization cue that is the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, where the ear without obstruction receives a stronger sound and the difference can indicate the direction from which the sound is coming.
An acoustic shadow is the occurrence in which a sound wave does not reach one ear, caused by an object in front of the sound source or by the position of the head.
Interaural time difference is a binaural sound localization cue from different sound arrival times at the ears, which can be used to locate the source.

Head-related transfer function (HRTF) is a model that describes how a listener receives sound from a location in space. It depends on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, so each person's is unique; an average listener's is used, and a pair for both ears can synthesize binaural sound and support localization in XR.

A see-through display is a display, typically good for mixed reality or augmented reality, that enables users to see and interact with the physical world while adding virtual objects to the real world or visually enhancing real objects, as a computer uses wearable device sensors to detect which real object the user is dealing with.
Human somatosensory system is a sensory system that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.
Kinesthesis is the awareness of the parameters associated with moving body parts, providing information on velocities, accelerations, and forces during movement.
Touch receptor is a human somatosensory receptor devoted to the sense of touch, embedded in the epidermis or dermis, that transforms touch into neural impulses for the brain.
The epidermis is the first layer of the skin, in which touch receptors are embedded.
The dermis is the second layer of the skin.
A muscle spindle is a receptor in the human somatosensory system that is embedded in muscles and reports changes in muscle length to the brain, supporting proprioception and kinesthesis.

A Golgi tendon organ is a receptor, used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system, that is embedded in tendons connecting muscles to bones and reports changes in muscle tension associated with movement.
A tendon is a body part that connects muscles to bones.

A joint receptor is a receptor used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system that is located at joints between bones, coordinates muscle movement, and provides information on relative bone positions.

Haptic perception is a major part of somatosensory perception that involves perceiving the overall geometric shape of objects through touch, at levels from input received by skin receptors to object manipulations called haptic explorations, and helps create mental models and improve the immersive experience in virtual environments.
Haptic exploration is the manipulation of geometric objects through touch that is used to form a mental model of their overall shape, size, weight, and hardness.
Enclosure is a type of haptic exploration needed for global shape or volume perception.
Contour following is a type of haptic exploration used for local shape perception.

Mental model is a spatial knowledge base of the surroundings and overall environment that consists of landmark, procedural, and topological knowledge to make locating oneself and identifying a suitable path easier.
Force feedback is the most popular form of touch sensation in extended reality, typically provided as vibrations by force feedback devices, particularly in virtual reality.

The KGS dot view model DV-2 is a haptic pin array with a matrix of pins that a computer controls, forcing them upward according to signals generated for objects in the virtual world to simulate the texture of an object surface when the user's fingertip scans across it.

A haptic pin array is a computer-controlled matrix of pins that are forced upward, according to signals generated for objects in the virtual world, to simulate the texture of an object surface when a user's fingertip scans across it.

Tangible user interface is a real-world object whose virtual avatar appears in a virtual world and that, by aligning the real world and the virtual world, provides feedback to the user's somatosensory system in place of computer-controlled haptic devices.

A chemical sense is a sense, such as taste or smell, whose chemoreceptors work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations, and not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli.
Smell-O-Vision is a system for adding smell to films in which odors were injected into movie theater seats at different points during a film according to the scenery.

A smell interface is an interface that provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose, with other components that help create the odor.
Room-scale delivery is the delivery of odor on a room scale for social or larger experiences.
A taste interface is an interface that can place electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation that simulates the main taste types.

Software development lifecycle (SDLC) is a systematic, structured set of connected stages for developing and deploying software, ideally followed in sequence but highly iterative for usable interactive systems, that captures design and development activities and helps identify the best valid design choice for usability.
Design space is a set of all possible designs.
A participant is a user selected for an experiment on the basis of a user profile so that the selected users form a representative sample of the whole user group.

A user-centric design approach is an approach to usable interactive systems and extended reality software that includes users' needs and expectations, requiring a highly iterative software development lifecycle with loops between stages.
Iteration is a cycle that returns to a previous stage of interactive system development to account for user feedback, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated, and refined until it is stabilized.
User feedback is the involvement of users in different ways, not only through feedback, that iterations between stages in an interactive system development lifecycle account for.

Requirement gathering is a stage of the interactive system development lifecycle that collects functional and non-functional requirements from clients and end users, focuses on end-user usability requirements, and specifies them for design, implementation, and deployment.

The design-prototype-evaluate cycle is a cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development that quickly prototypes, evaluates, and refines interface and interaction design, not code design, until the design stabilizes.

Early evaluation is an evaluation point in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle of the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development that quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time.

Code testing is a standard software development stage in interactive system development that evaluates code as part of coding and implementation by ensuring it is bug-free and executes properly, but does not establish whether the system is usable.

Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.
Requirement analysis is an analysis in the development of interactive systems that typically refers to the requirements of the client.

The design-prototype-evaluate loop is an iterative design loop for interactive systems in which an early design is prototyped, evaluated with user feedback, and refined through many quick iterations until few significantly different problems are identified. It includes interface and interaction design from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later activity.

Interface design is an activity in interactive system development that involves designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, uses a design-prototype-evaluate cycle, repeated with prototyping and quick evaluation until stable, and is separate from code design.

Interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC) is a staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical usability evaluation.
Executability is a quality of code in which the code is bug-free and executes properly.
Usability testing is a systematic empirical study that involves users to estimate whether an interactive system is usable, distinct from code testing, which only shows that a system is executable.

A virtual reality tour is a virtual reality experience for visiting a recreated place without physically going there, in which movement from one point to another is either user-controlled or system-controlled.

The Majuli case study is a virtual reality case study focused on designing, implementing, and evaluating an immersive interactive tour that digitally preserves the ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island.
Digital preservation is the use of digital media to preserve educational, scientific, and other resources.

Evaluation is a study of an extended reality system that measures usability aspects, such as user engagement, presence, and comfort, and identifies potential improvements by collecting end-user data through a controlled experiment and a structured questionnaire.
Majuli is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in Assam that is surrounded on all sides by the river and its tributaries and is considered the world's largest inhabited river island.
Monsoon season is the season in Majuli that typically runs from May to September.
The non-monsoon season is the season on Majuli that lasts from October to April.
A satra is a monastery on Majuli, Assam, that is an authoritative center of the Vaishnavite faith and a living workshop for visual and performing arts.
Tangible heritage is a form of heritage that someone can touch and feel.

Intangible heritage is heritage that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed, including traditional skills, knowledge, and aesthetic norms embedded in the daily and occasional activities of social life.
Ecological heritage is the flora and fauna that exist because of a natural formation's unique geology, geography, and topography.
Traditional preservation methods are methods for preserving cultural heritage, including oral traditions, museums, maintenance of historical sites, and documentation.
Archiving is storing visual and audio files that capture the heritage information of a particular entity, object, space, or place in digital heritage preservation.

Heritage preservation is creating an archive of heritage information using virtual reality (VR) and other immersive technologies, ideally a multimedia archive comprising images, videos, audio, and text, with images and videos in 2D and 360-degree forms, to preserve heritage for future generations.
A multimedia archive is an archive comprising images, videos, audio, and text, with images and videos in 2D and 360-degree forms, used for an immersive virtual tour or exploration of heritage.

The Majuli Island virtual reality tour is a heritage preservation tour focused mainly on the island's tangible and intangible cultural heritage, in which preservation produces tour content and immersive virtual tours let users explore the island, aiming to make them feel present and reduce cyber sickness.
Preservation is a component of a digital heritage preservation system that produces the content of a virtual tour.
Bihu is a traditional harvest festival of Assam.
Cultural landscape is the tangible and intangible cultural heritage of the Majuli island, represented by a map with hotspots.
A hotspot is a numbered place on a map of Majuli that represents a satra, village, town, or other place used to capture tangible and intangible cultural heritage.

A multimodal heritage archive is a collection of 2D and 360-degree images and videos, drone shots and videos, 3D models, and text that captures tangible and intangible heritage and is used to recreate a virtual landscape and virtual tour.
Testing is checking whether a design meets user requirements; it means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it.

Contextual inquiry (CI) is a usability requirement-gathering method, often described as a semi-structured interview process, that observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting and asks users questions to clarify behavior.
User requirement is an end-user requirement that ensures usability and is specified so it can be converted into plans for system design, implementation, and deployment.

System-centered design (SCD) is a design approach that makes the system, rather than the user, its main concern, with development driven by the developer's skill and interest, by what can be easily built on the platform, and by available tools rather than user needs and expectations.
Design stage is a stage in the interactive system development lifecycle that may involve interface design or code design.

Functional requirement (FR) is a formally specifiable requirement that specifies a system feature as a black-box function with a well-defined input and output, optionally its purpose, making it easy to convert into code.
Non-functional requirement (NFR) is a system characteristic that cannot be expressed as a function and is typically related to quality attributes of software.
A usability requirement is a type of non-functional requirement that concerns the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable.

Interface issue is a category of non-functional requirements that concerns interface design or usability, covering how a system interfaces with its environment, users, and other systems, including external hardware-software interfaces and user interfaces.
An external system interface is an interface between hardware and software.
A semi-structured interview is a process that consists of both interviews and observations.

Interview is the part of contextual inquiry that may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify behaviors or activities, and it is used to gather usability requirements and identify user groups.
A requirement is an end-user requirement that states what must be done to make a system usable, without specifying how to implement it; it can be functional or non-functional.
Active mode is a mode of contextual inquiry in which the observer is physically present in the environment where users are doing their tasks.

Passive mode is a mode of contextual inquiry in which no observer is present while users perform tasks, and their activities are recorded or videotaped for later observation, with issues clarified through interaction with the users.

The master-apprentice model is a model for genuine contextual inquiry in which the observer acts as an apprentice or learner, treats users as masters or teachers, and learns how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave, with advice prohibited.

Plan stage is the first stage of contextual inquiry that involves identifying observation goals, gathering task-domain knowledge, planning recording arrangements, identifying the users and date, time, and place of the observation, and scripting and rehearsing the procedure as a helpful practice.

Initiate stage is a stage of contextual inquiry that involves obtaining all necessary permissions from relevant authorities before observing employees in their workplace and opening communication with end users to remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them, so that they behave naturally.
The execute stage is a stage of contextual inquiry in which the actual inquiry takes place through performing observations and recording data.
Close stage is the fourth stage of contextual inquiry, in which the inquiry is formally closed, ideally by sending thank-you notes or a message of gratitude to users and, possibly, to authorities.
Reflect stage is the final stage of contextual inquiry in which the observer or experimental team analyzes data collected during the execute stage and identifies design goals.

Affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to analyze collected data by generating, displaying, sorting similar ideas into named groups, and drawing the finished diagram to reveal patterns for design recommendations.
A group header is a name or identifier assigned to a group in an affinity diagram after the ideas have been sorted, referring to the pattern that binds the ideas within the group.

Design guideline is a statement about an interactive system that says what should or should not be done to make it usable, without saying how to implement it; it can be generic or particular to a system, and is only a starting point to be implemented and tested.

An informed design choice is a design recommendation or guideline that is produced by analyzing data collected during a contextual inquiry, ensuring that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.
An uninformed design choice is a guideline created without contextual inquiry that does not ensure that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.
A function is a well-defined input-output unit that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, performs a specific task.
Functional specification is a specification of requirements in terms of functions that have well-defined inputs and outputs, making such requirements easier to convert to code.

Software requirements specification (SRS) is a textual document that specifies all of a system's requirements, both functional and non-functional, including the formal specification of its functional requirements.

A requirement hierarchy is a hierarchy in which requirements are generally organized in a software requirements specification, with identifiers distinguishing top-level requirements from sub-requirements, each representing a function with a clearly defined input and a clearly defined output.

A requirement identifier is an identifier in a software requirements specification hierarchy that represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does.
A sub-requirement is a requirement in a software requirements specification hierarchy that is generally identified by an identifier such as R1.1 under a top-level requirement.

The Majuli virtual reality tour is an immersive virtual reality case study tour for non-resident students, tourists, and pilgrims, intended to capture and digitally preserve the tangible and intangible heritage of Majuli river island.

Data subset restriction is a restriction that allows each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, based on what that group typically does, reducing the expanse of information and the possibility of cyber sickness.
Location information is information in a virtual reality tour that tells users where they are in the geographical space.
Location awareness is a wayfinding feature for ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.
An interaction aid is a virtual reality design aid that enhances user experience by providing navigation support, user-friendly interfaces, and natural interactions that increase presence.

Code design is one of two design stages in interactive system development, separate from interface and interaction design, and, like code design in other non-interactive software, it produces the design of the code using notations such as DFD, ER, object-oriented approaches, or UML before coding and testing.

Interface and interaction design is the design activity that addresses where or how to start the design process and how to express a design, which means having a design language, so it can be brainstormed and refined.
A design language is a specification of a design that expresses it so that it can be brainstormed and refined; there can be different languages for specifying a design.

Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are a set of eight generic design rules, primarily intended for graphical user interfaces, that can be partly or fully applied to other interactive systems, including extended reality (XR) systems.

A specific design guideline is a virtual reality-specific guideline for avoiding or minimizing cyber sickness that is typically applicable to virtual reality or immersive systems where immersion is very important, but may not apply to augmented reality systems.
Generic design guideline is a guideline applicable to any interactive system, including extended reality systems, although it is mostly, not fully, applicable to such systems.
A generic design rule is a design rule developed primarily for graphical user interfaces that can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces, including extended reality systems.
Consistency is a rule of system and interface design that calls for internal consistency and external or environmental consistency.

Internal consistency is a type of consistency in system design in which the same elements and interactions are used for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances, rather than separate objects, elements, or interactions.

External consistency is a type of consistency in system design in which the elements and interactions in a virtual world closely match the user's real-world experience and knowledge, so that real-world knowledge transfers to the virtual world.

Shneiderman's second golden rule is the rule that a system should be designed for universal usability by providing facilities for all user categories and supporting different user categories rather than only specific user categories.
Universal usability is a design rule requiring a system to provide facilities for all user categories and to support different user categories rather than only specific user categories.
Recall is a skilled task, as opposed to recognition, in which users may need to remember options rather than recognize them.
Informative feedback is feedback that, for user actions, tells the user what the system is doing, how much of a task is complete, or whether the action was completed successfully.
A progress bar is informative feedback that sometimes appears during a task, shows the percentage of the task completed, and gives the user a sense of how much longer to wait.

Closure is a result that is yielded by designing dialogues to organize task execution into beginning, middle, and end parts and providing feedback at the end of each group, so the user feels the task is started, executed, and completed.
Error prevention is a system design rule in which the design helps users prevent errors by aiming to keep error rates low, because user errors cannot be completely eliminated.
Error handling is a system design practice that, when an error occurs, gives simple, easy-to-understand information rather than complicated error messages.

Reversal of actions is a system design rule that permits users to return from an erroneous situation, ideally by keeping a reversal option available, with undo and redo facilities primarily meant to permit it.
A reversal option is a design option kept available so that users can return from an erroneous situation.
Keeping users in control is a usability rule that requires lay users to feel in control, perceive that their interaction changes the system state, and receive feedback on their actions and results.

Human memory is, in a broad sense, the combination of short-term and long-term memory, where short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.
Short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store that holds five to nine chunks of information at a time and is used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.

cards.front: seven plus or minus two rule
cards.back: Seven plus or minus two rule is a psychological finding that states the short-term memory limit is five to nine chunks of information at a time.
Short-term memory limit is the limit on the number of chunks of information that short-term memory can hold at a time, five to nine chunks.
A chunk of information is a unit of information that can be a letter, a word, a whole sentence, or a whole concept, depending on the application.

Reducing short-term memory load is a usability rule that requires keeping the information needed to operate an interface or perform an interaction between five and nine chunks, and not forcing users to remember more than nine.

Object interaction is a kind of interaction in immersive virtual environments that involves selecting one or more virtual objects in the environment and manipulating a selected object to change its properties.

Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.
Interaction for system control is an interaction technique in immersive environments that issues commands to change system state, mode, or system-related settings.
Object selection is an object interaction technique, typically used in immersive environments, that specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world.

Virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique for virtual objects, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it by a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation.
An immersive environment is an environment that, in the ideal case, blocks the user's senses and cuts the user off from the real world.

Object manipulation is an interaction technique in immersive environments that, typically after selection, modifies a virtual object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, or behavior.

A navigation technique is an interaction technique for moving from one point to another in a virtual world with a change in viewpoint, mostly without object interaction; it is broadly categorized as walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, or manipulation-based.

System control is a mostly regular type of interaction in immersive experiences that uses familiar computer-system techniques to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus.
Selection performance is the performance of a user while accomplishing an object selection task in a virtual experience, and a suitable object selection technique is chosen so that it is maximized.
A target object is an object to be selected in an object selection task in a virtual experience.
Target occlusion is the partial or full occlusion of a target by other surrounding objects, which can make locating and selecting the target challenging and may require specialized techniques.
Pointing-based selection is an object selection technique in a virtual world in which a user points a visible virtual ray from a hand, head, or eye to select the first object intersected by that ray.

Image plane selection is a two-dimensional selection technique in which the user selects on a view plane that contains the object as viewed from a distance and holds one or two hands or fingers between the eye and the object and provides a signal such as a gesture or hand movement when the object lines up.

Volumetric selection is an object selection technique in a virtual world that extends image plane selection by letting the user select a three-dimensional region, such as a box, sphere, or cone, and select the objects within it.

Hand selection technique is a technique that selects virtual objects in a virtual world by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch an object and trigger a grab, conventionally using one hand.

The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant virtual objects that uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, allows the user to change virtual arm and hand length interactively, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so distant objects can be reached quickly.

Prism technique is a travel technique for hand selection of virtual objects that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's physical hand moves below a specified speed, and keeps the virtual hand still when the hand velocity is below a minimum velocity.

Intent-driven selection is a grabbing hand selection technique in which a user moves a virtual hand toward an object and either positions virtual fingers or uses their posture around it to indicate the confidence level in selecting it, typically using proximity spheres that encompass multiple objects and reduce in size to refine the selection to a specific object.
One-to-one mapping is a mapping of a physical hand's motion and orientation to a virtual hand, tying the virtual hand to the physical hand and allowing natural hand movements.
Virtual arm length is the length of the virtual hand.

A proximity sphere is a selection area used by intent-driven selection techniques that encompasses multiple objects at a larger distance and progressively reduces in size, depending on hand or finger postures, as the user moves closer, refining the selection to a specific object.

Virtual ray is a short line segment or infinite line attached to a virtual hand, head, or eye that a user extends in pointing-based selection to point at objects and select the first intersected object.
Hand pointing is a form of pointing for pointing-based selection that is done with a hand or a handheld input device, and it can trigger selection in methods that combine it with gaze pointing.
Head pointing is pointing for pointing-based selection in which a head-mounted display extends a ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand.
Eye-gaze pointing is a pointing method for pointing-based selection that uses an eye tracker.
Ray casting is the most basic pointing-based selection method in which the user points at objects with a virtual ray.

Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely; a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending.

Depth ray is an improved ray-casting technique that uses a user-controlled depth marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, to disambiguate multiple intersected objects and select the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

A depth marker is a user-controlled marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, that disambiguates multiple intersected objects and selects the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

Head crusher technique is an image plane selection technique in which the user positions the thumb and forefinger so that they surround or enclose the desired object in the two-dimensional image plane.
Sticky finger technique is an image plane selection technique in which the object underneath the user's finger is selected.

The lifting palm technique is an image plane selection technique in which a user selects an object by flattening an outstretched hand and positioning the palm below the object as if trying to lift it with the palm.
The framing hands technique is an image plane selection technique in which the user positions hands to form the two corners of a frame in a two-dimensional image surrounding an object.

The cone casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique that extends ray casting by casting a cone instead of a ray to a distance and selecting objects within the cone, so it can select multiple objects, though selecting smaller or tightly grouped objects may be difficult.
The sphere casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique that casts a sphere onto the nearest intersected surface and selects the objects found within that sphere.

Two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique that uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of 3D space.

Hand manipulation is a manipulation technique that uses a virtual hand to manipulate objects and is implemented using smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction; it is the most intuitive way of manipulating objects.

Indirect manipulation is a manipulation technique sometimes used for virtual objects in which the user does not directly manipulate the virtual object with the physical hand, but manipulates other objects mapped to the virtual object, and the mapped objects manipulate the virtual object.

A three-dimensional widget is a simple indirect manipulation technique that places controls directly in a 3D scene with virtual objects, so manipulating a widget manipulates its associated object; each widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom.

Indirect proxy is an indirect manipulation technique that lets the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop, so that moving it moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

World in miniature (WIM) is an indirect proxy that provides a miniature handheld model of a virtual environment, representing all objects in the virtual world. Manipulating a model object manipulates the corresponding virtual object, even if it is outside the user's reach; moving certain model objects can also change the virtual viewpoint.

Miniature model is a handheld model of a virtual environment that represents all objects in the environment, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding object in the virtual environment.

A bimanual manipulation technique is a technique for manipulating objects with both hands, in which hand movement is synchronous, with both hands moving together, or asynchronous, where the hands do not need to move simultaneously.
Synchronous is a hand movement in a bimanual manipulation technique in which both hands move together.
Asynchronous is a kind of hand movement in a bimanual manipulation technique in which both hands do not need to move simultaneously.

Spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle for moving or rotating a virtual world object.
A virtual spindle is a virtual object defined by two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously.

Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric but synchronous technique that extends the spindle technique by moving both hands together without requiring them to be symmetrically placed around the sides of an imaginary axis.

An integrated hybrid manipulation technique is a technique that automatically switches from selection to manipulation after selection, without an explicit user signal, and switches back to selection mode after manipulation, so selection and manipulation are not performed separately.

cards.front: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER)
cards.back: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER) is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique in which the user selects an object by ray casting, the virtual hand automatically moves to and attaches to the object instead of the ray attaching, and hand manipulation changes the object’s position and orientation until the user ends it with a trigger or gesture.
Locomotion technique is a technique that lets a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and perceive that travel has taken place.

Wayfinding is the component of navigation, other than locomotion or travel, that provides location awareness, ascertains a path to a destination, transfers spatial knowledge to the real world, and builds a mental model of the environment.
Exploration is a kind of travel in navigation that has no explicit goal or target point, where the user moves around to see, learn, or explore.
Search is a way of traveling in navigation that involves moving to a specified target location.
Maneuvering is a type of travel in navigation that comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination.

Walking-based locomotion is a locomotion technique for traveling in a virtual environment in which physical walking or movement in the physical world is mapped to corresponding movement in the virtual environment, and it is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

Selection-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user selects where to go rather than continuously specifying how to move there by steering or looking. Its two types are target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion; route planning-based locomotion has the user select a route to the target rather than only the endpoint.

Manipulation-based locomotion is a type of locomotion technique in which the user's position, orientation, or scale is manipulated using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world.

Full gait technique is a walking-based locomotion technique that is the most natural way to travel and in which the user's actual real-world walking, restricted within a specified physical limit, is translated into any amount of virtual movement in a potentially infinite virtual space, creating a mismatch between physical and virtual movement.

A partial gait technique is a walking-based locomotion technique in which the user walks in place without changing position, requiring specialized devices to map the pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.
