A gait negation technique is a walking-based virtual locomotion technique that requires a specialized setup to cancel the user's lateral movements and keep the user's physical position fixed before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation.

Steering-based navigation is a navigation category in which direction and speed are continuously controlled while the user moves from one point to another. Its two types are spatial steering-based navigation, controlled by the user's body parts, and physical steering-based navigation, controlled by vehicular props or additional hardware.
Spatial steering-based navigation is a type of steering-based navigation that is controlled using the user's body parts. It can be gaze-directed, hand-directed, or body-leaning directed.

Physical steering-based navigation is a type of steering-based navigation that uses physical setups, vehicular props, or additional hardware, in which physically moving the steering controls causes travel in the virtual world.
Gaze-directed is a form of spatial steering-based navigation in which looking at a target location moves the user continuously in the direction of looking.
Hand-directed is a form of spatial steering-based navigation in which hand gestures determine the direction of travel.
Body-leaning directed is a kind of spatial steering-based navigation in which leaning the body toward a movement direction is mapped to corresponding travel.

Target selection-based locomotion is a type of selection-based locomotion in which the user selects a destination or target, and the virtual viewpoint changes so that the user feels moved to that target.

Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint, moving along that route through changing viewpoints.
Map dragging is a target selection-based locomotion technique in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly.

Spatial knowledge is the essential knowledge base of a wayfinding mental model, comprising landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment.
Environment design is the design of an environment whose objective is to make it easier for the user to build a mental map.

A wayfinding mental model is a mental model whose essential knowledge base is spatial knowledge, consisting of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment.
Procedural knowledge is knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path.
Topological knowledge is the spatial knowledge of the overall environment in a wayfinding mental model.

A knowledge base is the essential collection of spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model, formed by landmark knowledge of surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment.

Wayfinding support is essential support in complex virtual environments that helps users find targets by using landmarks, maps, colored paths, breadcrumb trails, or direction indicators, so travel techniques can be used effectively.

Landmark support is wayfinding support that uses obvious, distinct, non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

A landmark is an obvious, distinct, non-mobile object positioned in a given place that supports wayfinding, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.
Map support is wayfinding support that can provide maps of the virtual space or place.

A world in miniature display is a display for wayfinding that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points.
Path following support is a wayfinding support that can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.

Breadcrumb support is support for wayfinding that leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.
A compass is a direction indicator that can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space.
A command is a regular operation in software use that changes system state or mode, such as launching an application, changing system settings, or opening a file.
A graphical menu is an adapted two-dimensional menu suitable for three-dimensional massive environments, used as an interactive method for system control.
A multimodal interaction technique is an interactive method for system control that combines multiple techniques.

Design is the interface and interaction design part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle in interactive system development, not code design, that may be based on intuition, design guidelines, or team brainstorming, and is refined through prototyping and quick evaluation until stable.
A textual description is descriptive text that provides additional context about locations, significant spots, artifacts, objects, or elements in a virtual tour or multimodal archive.

A minimap is a local world-in-miniature map of a specific place, distinct from a global map, that shows the arrangement of 360-degree images as white dots, with the current image highlighted green, to support local orientation and wayfinding.
A tutorial video is a video that explains to users how to control and use a system.
Boat ride experience is the opening part of a virtual tour that uses a 360-degree boat ride video to give the user the feeling of being transported by boat from one river bank to the other.
Preprocessing is a process for collected images and videos that improves their visual appearance and the user's quality of experience by using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements.

Tablet interface is a virtual interface that serves as the main interface in a virtual tour system, providing navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content, with a design inspired by real-world tablet use.
A navigation tool is a tool provided by a virtual tablet interface, such as a left-side island map presented as a world in miniature and buttons for opening a mini map.

A video player is a part of a virtual tablet interface in a virtual tour that lets users view cultural or ecological videos relevant to their current location, including 360-degree, drone, or 2D videos, with a volume controller and other controls.
An island map is a world-in-miniature map that shows the entire island or a specific place on it to provide location awareness, wayfinding, and orientation awareness.

A navigation arrow is an arrow shown to a user that indicates which way to move and, when selected, moves the user in that direction from one 360-degree image to another, guiding the user toward points of interest and preventing random movement.

Notification is an informative alert or textual description in a virtual tour that tells users whether a cultural video or activity is available at a location, shown through an information icon or tablet interface.

An information icon is an icon in a virtual tour that becomes active at a point of interest and, when selected, provides further details about that place, mostly as textual information, including whether a cultural video is available.

Dual maps are two maps used by a system for location awareness: a global world-in-miniature map of the entire island on a tablet interface and a local minimap on a local interface, reducing clutter and providing clear navigation support.
An island tour is a tour in which each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another.
View interpolation is a method that blurs the boundaries between two 360-degree images to ensure a smooth visual transition and prevent sudden movement or jerks.
A virtual vehicle metaphor is a three-dimensional (3D) model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within a tour.

The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which a pre-planned route is chosen by selecting a destination, not by target selection or instantaneous movement; it gives the user a seated viewpoint inside a vehicle, changes surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create motion, and uses ray casting interactions for direction and destination.
Route selection is a selection-based locomotion technique, not target selection or instantaneous movement, in which the user selects a destination to select a pre-planned route.

A virtual tour system is a virtual-world system that provides a tablet interface for location-relevant videos and spot-specific video lists, as well as textual place descriptions and point-of-interest guidance using directional arrows and information icons.

Controlled navigation technique is a navigation technique in which users navigate or teleport using a joystick, so that controlled movement does not support abrupt movements that can cause cybersickness.

A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that can be built quickly to model or demonstrate a design idea and to test whether it will work in practice. It can be discarded after testing or refined into the final product.

Quick evaluation is the stage of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle in the interactive system development lifecycle that evaluates a prototype, may use methods such as cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation, and the results of the evaluation are used to refine the design until it stabilizes.

A cycle is a repeated loop of stages in an interactive system development lifecycle; the design-prototype-evaluate cycle refines a design based on evaluation results until the design stabilizes, and other cycles may connect code design, coding, implementation, code testing, usability evaluation, requirement gathering, or interface design.

Experience design is an iterative design process whose design-prototype-evaluate cycle consists of designing, quickly prototyping, evaluating, finding problems, refining, and repeating with new prototypes and evaluations until the design stabilizes.

Full implementation is a complete implementation of a software idea that involves highly skilled programmers and many cost components, including setting up or procuring resources and engaging manpower.

Horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing its look, feel, and appearance without functionality or interaction, so it is used to discuss, brainstorm, and elicit feedback about whether the interface is understandable, intuitive, and usable.

A vertical prototype is a type of prototype that implements a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in depth, from the first screen to the last, to represent interactions rather than all system functionalities.

A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype of an interface made without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and to represent interaction it needs a series of interface sketches, often called a storyboard, rather than a single sketch.

Low-fidelity prototyping is a prototyping approach that provides a quick and cheap way to make and modify prototypes, does not rely on computers or digital media, and uses a series of interface sketches, a practice often called storyboarding, to brainstorm alternative designs and obtain user feedback on usability, primarily for horizontal prototypes but also for vertical prototypes.

An interface sketch is a simple drawing that can be made on paper and depicts an interface’s major components, appearance, and layout. It expresses an interface idea for comments and feedback. A single drawing gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series can give a vertical prototype of interaction.

A storyboard is a low-fidelity prototype consisting of a series of interface sketches, each a keyframe, that captures the sequence of user actions and screen changes for a specific task from beginning to end.
A keyframe is a snapshot of an interaction at a particular point in time that, in a storyboard, visualizes the interaction for a specific task and its scenes.

Medium-fidelity prototyping is a prototyping approach that uses a computer to create simple prototypes without coding, primarily for horizontal prototypes as static interface sketches without real functionality and for vertical prototypes as animations or slideshows that simulate interaction.

High-fidelity prototyping is a sophisticated prototyping approach that uses computer programs or programming, effectively reduced-scale software development requiring skilled programmers, and requires much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping and is primarily suited to vertical prototypes rather than horizontal ones.

The wizard of Oz approach is a prototype-creation technique in which a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer, but an unseen human operator called the wizard operates the computer and returns the requested response or result.
A wizard is an unseen human operator in a Wizard of Oz prototype who operates the computer and returns the requested response to a subject who believes the computer is autonomous.

The listening typewriter experiment is a Wizard of Oz test of a speech recognition idea in which a user spoke to a computer believed to be real, a hidden person typed what was heard, and text appeared on the user’s screen as if automatically recognized.
A throwaway prototype is a prototype that is easy and fast to create, is used for quick evaluation, and is then discarded.

An incremental prototype is a kind of prototype that is created by dividing a system into units or modules, separately prototyping and testing each module, and integrating the modules into the overall system.

An evolutionary prototype is a prototype created by prototyping and testing the whole system, starting with a simpler version, refining it, adding more functionalities, and altering it based on testing results until it becomes the final product, rather than by prototyping separate modules and combining them.

A module is a part into which a system design divides a system for an incremental prototype, and each module is prototyped and tested separately before the modules are integrated into the overall system.

Expert evaluation is a quick, cheap usability test of a prototype at an early design stage, in which design-team members or domain experts independently report usability issues, and a few end users may be included optionally.
A robust evaluation technique is an evaluation technique that typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.
An evaluator is a skilled person who examines a prototype and reports usability issues or heuristic violations.

An evaluation team is a group, mainly the design team or domain experts and optionally a few end users, used to assess a prototype in quick or expert evaluation, with expert evaluations using three to five members who assess independently.
Usability issue is a problem in the usability of an interface or prototype that evaluators identify during evaluations, and that users are likely to face while performing tasks.

Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert usability inspection method in which evaluators identify problems by performing interface-level tasks converted from a scenario on at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, guided by usability questions framed in advance.
Usability inspection is a method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.
A low-fidelity vertical prototype is a prototype that supports several tasks and is the minimum required for a cognitive walkthrough.
A paper prototype is a simple, low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough, made as a storyboard: a series of sketches showing screen changes after each interaction.
A scenario is a description of a task created for evaluators in a cognitive walkthrough, whose described task is converted into the actions that must be performed in a prototype.
Interface-level task is an action that must be performed in a prototype to accomplish a task described in a scenario.

A usability question is a question framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues; evaluators use it as a guideline to identify likely user problems and must answer it with a detailed report rather than a simple yes-or-no response.

A report is a detailed answer that evaluators give for each usability question, rather than a simple yes or no answer, explaining where difficulty was felt in an interface or interaction and why, and it is collected, combined, and analyzed to identify broader usability issues.

Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to identify usability problems across the whole system at an early design stage.

A checklist is a list of heuristics used in heuristic evaluation to assess a prototype or interface by checking whether each heuristic is followed or violated. Checklists can be detailed and system-specific, or focused on broader usability principles, and broader checklists contain fewer heuristics.
A broader checklist is a checklist for evaluating interfaces that focuses on broader usability principles, contains fewer heuristics, and is not specific to any particular interface.

Nielsen's ten heuristics is a general set of usability heuristics, primarily for graphical user interfaces but applicable to most interactive systems. It consists of: visibility of system status, real-world match, user control, consistency, error prevention, recognition over recall, flexibility, minimal design, error recovery, and help and documentation. It is used to identify usability problems early from low-fidelity prototypes.
Visibility of system status is a heuristic that says the status of a system should be visible to the user.

cards.front: match between system and the real world
cards.back: Match between system and the real world is a heuristic stating that what a user does on a system should closely match the user's real-world experience.
User control and freedom is a heuristic that concerns whether a user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided.
Consistency and standards is a heuristic in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed.

Recognition rather than recall is a heuristic in which a user should not have to remember what to do, but should be able to recognize from elements what to do, because recollection is more difficult than recognition.
Aesthetic and minimalist design is a heuristic in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing.
Help and documentation is a heuristic in which a system should provide help and documentation support.
The Cyber Sickness Questionnaire (CSQ) is a questionnaire relevant to cyber sickness in extended reality that is good for evaluating virtual reality experiences with head-mounted displays.
Google Cardboard is a head-mounted display in which a smartphone is inserted to provide a 360-degree virtual reality experience.
User evaluation is a quick evaluation technique that obtains feedback by asking users directly using rating scales, and it requires user involvement.
Subjective data is user feedback data collected with rating scales in user evaluation.
A questionnaire is a set of questions or statements provided to users to rate in user evaluation, although it need not contain questions.
Post-task data collection is the collection of user evaluation data after each task, using suitable questionnaires.

After scenario questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire in which users rate three statements about satisfaction with ease of completing tasks, time taken to complete tasks, and support information on a seven-point scale.

System usability scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire containing ten statements, not questions, that users rate on a five-point agreement scale after completing all tasks, giving a quick percentage indication of whether a system has usability problems.
A seven-point rating scale is a rating scale for statements that ranges from 1 to 7, with 1 indicating strong disagreement and 7 indicating strong agreement.
A post-session questionnaire is a questionnaire that contains statements rather than questions and is administered at the end of a session after users have completed all tasks.
A five-point agreement scale is a rating scale in which 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree.

The System Usability Scale score (SUS score) is a usability score calculated from all ten statement ratings and interpreted directly as a percentage, with 70% or higher typically indicating an interface is usable or has only minimal problems.
A statement rating is a user's rating of one System Usability Scale statement on a 5-point agreement scale, used to calculate a System Usability Scale score.
Aesthetic survey questionnaire (ASQ) is a generic questionnaire applicable to any interactive system, not specifically meant for extended reality (XR) systems.
A 360-degree image tour is an implementation of the Majuli virtual reality tour that uses 360-degree images, cultural videos, 360-degree videos, and ambient sound.

The three-dimensional model tour is an implementation of the Majuli virtual reality tour that uses three-dimensional models textured from real images, rather than 360-degree images and videos, to create a realistic-looking appearance.

Mobile-device tour is the Google Cardboard implementation of the Majuli VR tour, a reduced form of the full Oculus Quest experience that uses a smartphone to provide a 360-degree experience, with simpler controls and fewer features.
A vehicle-metaphor route-planning method is a route-planning method in which the road route is fixed and the user experiences motion as if riding a vehicle along the road.

A quick prototype evaluation is a limited-scale early evaluation that uses a limited number of evaluators to evaluate prototypes, so it can quickly identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about the overall usability of the end system.

A research question is a question formulated in the first stage of an empirical study, which the experiment is conducted to answer and on which data collection and analysis are based, and it should avoid generalized concepts that make it untestable.

A variable is an item in a testable research question that is identified after the research questions are formulated, without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed; its two most important types are independent variables, or factors, that can take levels or values, and dependent variables that depend on those factors and levels.
An experiment is the designed and executed part of an empirical study that collects and compares objective data to answer a research question and measure the usability of an implemented interface.
Empirical data is data collected in an experiment or empirical study that answers a research question, and it is processed and tested for statistical significance before conclusions are drawn.
Text entry speed is objective data that is logged as characters per minute (CPM) and used to determine which text entry interface is faster.
Characters per minute (CPM) is an objective measure of text entry speed that records users' input speed and allows CPM values to be compared to determine which interface is faster.
A testable research question is a research question that allows a study to collect objective data and draw reliable conclusions independent of users' subjective interpretation.

A non-testable research question is a broader, generalized research question that cannot be directly tested objectively because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot collect objective data and a reliable scientific conclusion generally cannot be drawn.
An independent variable is a variable whose values are assigned and controlled; these values are called levels and are used to design an experiment.
A level is a value assigned to an independent variable or factor in an experiment.
A test condition is a combination of factor levels that is used to design an experiment.
A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels.

Research question framing is the first stage of the empirical research process that addresses broader generalizable but untestable questions by framing multiple testable research questions, collecting objective data for each, reaching definite conclusions for each, and combining those conclusions to draw a conclusion about the untestable questions.

Data analysis is the fourth stage of the system implementation process in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about a design's efficacy.
Sample is a subset of all potential users chosen for an experiment or empirical study to represent the larger population, so conclusions about that population are valid.
A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds.
A homogeneous subset is a user group whose members have the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds.
A user profile is a set of well-defined user characteristics or entries that, in experiment design, defines a user and is the only basis for selecting experiment participants.
A user profile characteristic is one of the well-defined elements of a user profile that, in experiment design, defines a user and is the only basis for selecting experiment participants.
Task performance data are mostly objective data collected from users performing tasks in a controlled experiment evaluating an interface, and are analyzed to draw conclusions about the interface.

A representative task set is a small, well-defined subset of the tasks that potential users most frequently or commonly use when an interface is deployed in practice, from which empirical studies ideally choose one or more tasks so that collected data and drawn conclusions are reliable.

Within-subject design is an experimental design in which every participant performs tasks corresponding to all test conditions; because repeated practice can confound the analysis, the task sequence may be randomized or systematically varied to reduce the practice effect.
Between-subjects design is an experimental design in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.

Practice effect is, in a within-subject design, an improvement in task performance from repeated practice that is a confounding variable and adds noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than the interface.
A Latin square design is a design that systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant.
An empirical interface study is an interface study that obtains data from a sample of users rather than the actual population and draws conclusions about a larger population.
A statistical significance test is a test that indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions.
A statistically significant difference is an observed difference in data that a statistical significance test indicates is not due to chance.
A non-significant difference is an observed data difference that is due to chance rather than to the tested conditions.
P-value is a probability in a statistical significance test that the data were obtained by chance, with a lower value meaning the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.
One-way analysis of variance is a parametric test used in between-subject designs for one factor with more than two levels.
Factorial analysis of variance is a parametric test used for between-subject designs with two or more factors, each having two or more levels.

The questionnaire for environmental presence (QEP) is a questionnaire used to measure presence. It is a revised version of the standard presence questionnaire and includes 19 core items and 3 optional sound-related items, answered on a 1-to-7 Likert scale.

A pre-experiment training session is a brief session before a VR experiment that demonstrates the features and use of the system used in the experiment, bringing participants to the same level and reducing or nullifying familiarity or prior-experience bias.
Prior-experience bias is a bias in a virtual reality experiment that may lead to incorrect conclusions when unfamiliar users produce results much different from familiar users.
A pre-exposure assessment is an assessment completed before exposure to a system.
Implementation is a stage in interactive system development that involves coding followed by code testing.

Stable interface design is an interface design in interactive system development that is reached after repeating a design-prototype-evaluate cycle until further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.
Primary-level testing is a form of code testing in implementation that may be review-based.
Secondary-level testing is a level of code testing that may be more systematic or structured than primary-level testing.

Agile development is a development framework that starts small, avoids collecting all requirements initially, and adds features over successive iterations to deliver projects quickly that are acceptable to clients. Its process flow consists of conceptualization, inception, iteration or sprint, release, production, and retirement.
Conceptualization is a part of the agile development process flow; together with inception, it roughly refers to physical feasibility study and requirement gathering.
Inception is a stage of the agile development process flow in which the team is created and funds and resources are arranged.
Sprint is a stage in the agile development process that typically requires four to six weeks and includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery.
Release is a stage in an agile development process in which testing, training, documentation, and deployment occur.
Production is a stage of the agile development process that involves ongoing support and maintenance after delivery.
Retirement is the stage of the agile development process flow that covers end-of-life activities.
Delivery is a part of an agile sprint in which the system is delivered to production, and agile development adds features over successive deliveries.

Virtual reality content is a set of external content factors that can induce cybersickness, such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.
Walking-based technique is a virtual locomotion technique that involves physical walking to move from one point to another in a virtual reality tour.

Optimization is the balancing of psychophysiological experience and resource utilization in an extended reality system so that immersive experience is maximized while resource requirements and cybersickness are minimized.

Psychophysiological experience optimization is a perspective of optimization in virtual reality that is roughly taken to mean designing the experience to minimize cyber sickness or the possibility of its induction.

Resource optimization is the technological optimization of resource requirements in extended reality (XR), including virtual reality (VR), that minimizes those requirements while maximizing immersive experience without compromising it. It generally focuses on client-end hardware so users can have a good experience with affordable hardware.
A user-controlled virtual reality tour is a virtual reality tour in which the user controls how and where to navigate using controllers or other input modalities.

A system-controlled virtual reality tour is a navigation mode in a virtual reality tour in which the system or application controls the user's movement, often along a predetermined path or sequence of movements.
Optic flow is the rate at which the visual scene changes, producing the perception of movement as the view of the surroundings changes.
A walking speed model is a model of a user's typical walking behavior that is used to match a system-controlled virtual reality tour's optic flow to the user's instantaneous walking speed.
A realistic walking behavior model is a model that can be used for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation to address the need for a realistic walking experience.

The corridor experiment is an experiment that used a corridor in a physical building in which seven paintings representing images of the seven wonders of the world were placed at distances from the start.
Video recording is a recording of a user's footsteps made with a camera fixed on the user's back and focused on the user's legs.
Instantaneous step frequency is the number of steps per second, where a step is one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground.
A step is an interval that extends from one foot strike on the ground to the next foot strike on the ground.

The slow-in-slow-out pattern is a pattern in step frequency plotted against distance in which step frequency starts low, increases to a maximum, plateaus, and then decreases to zero at a target where the user stops.

A slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is a walking pattern that starts, remains approximately constant, and returns to zero, like a square pulse wave, and is modeled by a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids with weights calculated from empirical data.

Fourier series is a weighted sum of harmonically related sinusoids that can approximate any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision, with practical approximations using the first few terms.
A square pulse wave is a wave that has a Fourier-series approximation that starts, remains approximately constant, and then returns to zero.
Actual movement speed is the user's movement speed in virtual walking, which is related to instantaneous step frequency and may differ from perceived movement speed.

Perceived movement speed is the perceived speed of scene change in virtual walking; it is not necessarily the same as actual movement speed, users generally perceive it more slowly than actual movement speed, and it is computed as a visual gain times that actual speed.
Visual gain is a factor in a natural walking speed model that multiplies actual instantaneous walking speed to compute the desired perceived scene-change speed.
Initial frequency is the frequency f0, equal to 1/(2d), where d is the distance between source and destination.

Natural walking speed model is a model for a system-controlled virtual reality tour that displays a visual speed, or optic flow, matching the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed by multiplying actual instantaneous walking speed by a visual gain factor, to provide a realistic walking experience.

Algorithm is the minimum-time path computation that takes a graph, converts it to a complete time-weighted graph, solves a travelling salesman problem, and replaces hypothetical edges with shortest paths in the original graph.
Speed is a distance element divided by an instantaneous time, expressed as dx/dt.

Perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual speed a user perceives in the natural walking-speed model and equals the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed.
Perception of movement is a perception that a virtual reality tour produces by displaying optic flow that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed.
Virtual world size is the geographical area of a virtual environment that a user needs to cover while traveling and exploring.

Travel time is the duration that moving between vertices in a virtual world takes, calculated from their distance and a natural walking-speed model; for a path, it is the sum of the times between consecutive vertices.
Interaction time is the time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects in virtual reality.
A system-controlled virtual reality tool is a virtual reality tool in which users do not interact with virtual objects.

A semi-interactive tour is a system-controlled virtual reality navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact only with a small set of objects at points of interest after a navigation task, and cannot interact with other objects.

A system-controlled navigation scenario is a virtual reality navigation scenario in which travel is automatic and users may interact only with a limited set of objects at points of interest after a navigation task is complete.

A semi-interactive virtual tour is a virtual tour in which interaction time at each point of interest can be limited in advance, after which the system automatically forces the user to move to another point of interest.

An optimum path is a navigation path in virtual reality that, under a limit on interaction time, either minimizes total navigation and interaction time to experience all points of interest or maximizes the number of points of interest experienced within a fixed time limit.

Original graph is the weighted graph input to an optimal-path algorithm that represents a virtual world, with vertices as points of interest, directly connected edges weighted by Euclidean distance, connected but not necessarily complete, and importance and waiting time specified for each node.
Vertex set is the set of all points of interest, represented as vertices, in a weighted graph that represents a virtual world.
A weighted edge is an edge between points of interest in a weighted graph that represents a top view of a virtual world.

Edge weight is a number assigned to a graph edge that represents the Euclidean distance for directly connected vertices, a very large number for non-directly connected vertices initially, the shortest path length after modification, or travel time in the final time-weighted graph.

The optimum travel path problem is the problem of finding a path in a given graph that covers all vertices, the points of interest, in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed throughout so the user gets a realistic feeling.

Instantaneous time is the time for a distance element, calculated as that element divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed, and integrated over a distance to give total travel time.
Travel-time estimate is the estimated travel time for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model, computed using a Fourier-series expansion.
V naught is a constant for a given user height, used in the travel-time estimate for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model.

Travel-time minimisation problem is a graph problem, a variation of the travelling salesman problem, whose objective is to find a path containing all vertices with the minimum total travel time. The graph is connected and not assumed to be a complete graph; for vertices not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is weighted by the shortest path length.

Travelling salesman problem (TSP) is a problem that, given a complete graph, asks for the shortest path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node, where the shortest path is defined by the total weight of the edges in the path.
A complete graph is a graph in which every pair of vertices is connected by an edge; where a direct edge is absent, a hypothetical edge representing the shortest path between the vertices is used.
Shortest path is a path between two vertices in a graph that has the least total weight of its edges.
A hamiltonian path is a path that covers all nodes and visits each node exactly once.

A hypothetical edge is an edge introduced between two vertices not directly connected in a graph used for travel-time minimisation, representing the shortest path between them for travel-time computation.

Modified edge weight is a computed weight for a direct or hypothetical edge between two vertices in a graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem, equal to the Euclidean distance for direct edges and to the shortest path length for hypothetical edges.
Shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path between two vertices in a connected graph.
Optimal time is the amount of time taken by the path that covers all vertices of a graph in the least time.
A complete time-weighted graph is a complete graph whose edge weights are travel times between vertex pairs rather than Euclidean distances, and it can be solved to obtain an optimal path.

A travelling salesman problem solver is a standard solver that takes a complete time-weighted graph as input and outputs the optimum time and optimal path; its optimal path may contain hypothetical edges that are replaced by shortest paths in the original graph.

Minimum-time approach is a cybersickness-minimizing approach that models a virtual world as a graph of points of interest, completes it with shortest-path travel times from the natural walking-speed model, and solves a TSP to find the minimum-time path covering all points of interest.
Final solution path is the path produced after removing hypothetical edges from the optimal path produced by a travelling salesman problem solver.

Optimal path is a path through points of interest that maximizes the total importance of the points visited and the number of the most important points covered while keeping total traveling and waiting time below a time threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur.

Time threshold (TTH) is the maximum duration of user movement, experience, or virtual reality exposure in a virtual tour, beyond which cybersickness may occur; it is the upper time limit used when optimizing a tour path.

A time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach is an optimization approach that seeks an optimal path covering the maximum number of points of interest (POIs) while completing within a time threshold (TTH).
Importance is a positive real number assigned to each node, vertex, or point of interest, and larger values indicate higher importance for determining which nodes to cover within a time threshold.
An importance function is a function that maps every node, vertex, or point of interest to a positive real number, with a larger number indicating higher importance.
Total importance is the sum of the individual importances of the nodes in a path.

Virtual reality path optimization model is a model in which each node, a point of interest, has an importance and a waiting time, the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and a path's total importance is maximized subject to total completion time plus waiting time not exceeding a time threshold.

Waiting time is the maximum time, represented by a positive real number, that a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at a node in a virtual reality path optimization model; total waiting time for a path is the sum of the nodes' waiting times.

The waiting time function is a function in a virtual reality path optimization formulation that maps each node, a point of interest, to the positive real number representing the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node.
Total waiting time is the sum of the individual waiting times of the vertices of a path in the revised virtual reality path optimization problem.

Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem, an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit, the importance of the nodes, within a time constraint.
Profit is the importance of nodes in the vehicle routing problem with profit; a route maximizes it within a time constraint when not all nodes must be visited.

Optimal-path algorithm is an algorithm for a virtual environment that finds a path covering the most important points of interest while keeping total travel and waiting time below a threshold; it completes the input graph with shortest paths, replaces Euclidean edge weights with natural walking-model travel times, and expands the chosen path into original-graph paths.
Total exposure time is the traveling time plus the waiting time for a path.

A modified optimal path is the path an algorithm returns after modifying the optimal path from a solver by replacing each hypothetical edge between two vertices with the shortest path between those vertices in the original graph.
A field study is a kind of contextual inquiry in which user behavior is observed and recorded, and users are interviewed to understand who they are and how they behave.
An edge is a connection between two nodes or vertices in a graph, which can be weighted by a distance or by a shortest path length.

cards.front: vehicle routing problem with profit solver
cards.back: A vehicle routing problem with profit solver is a solver that, given a graph and the importance and waiting time of each node, finds an optimal path within a chosen time threshold that maximizes the importance of the nodes covered while accounting for their maximum wait times.

Optimal path approach is a virtual reality navigation optimization approach that identifies a path letting a user explore all points of interest in minimum time, and it can be used to propose optimized navigation paths to maximize user experience.

Navigation optimization is a VR navigation approach: its first approach identifies a path for exploring all points of interest in minimum time, and its second approach assigns relative importance and maximum wait times to point-of-interest nodes when that time exceeds a threshold.

cards.front: optimal path under a time constraint approach
cards.back: Optimal path under a time constraint approach is an approach for walking-based virtual reality exploration that sets an upper time limit, called the time threshold, and within that duration identifies an optimized navigation path covering the maximum number of most important points of interest, including interacting with or inspecting them and navigating between them, to maximize user experience.
Covering is the process in a virtual tour that involves interacting with or inspecting points of interest and navigating from one to another.
Auniati Satra is a Satra on Majuli explored in a virtual reality tour.
Maximum wait time is the time a user needs to stop at a point of interest, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation.

Display controller is the rendering component in a generic graphics system that is responsible for image generation, receives display commands from the CPU, uses a GPU for rendering, and sends the generated two-dimensional digital image to video memory.

The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.
A pixel is an element in the grid of a graphic display screen that, when activated, emits light with a specific intensity, helping to form a colored image perceived on the screen.
Color is an observed combination of different amounts of red, green, and blue light emitted by the pixel elements of a color display and mixed in the eye.

An image is the whole interface displayed on a computer screen, not only the main object, comprising geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them.
Resource is any hardware, software, manpower, or supporting infrastructure required for extended reality (XR), particularly virtual reality (VR).

The client end is the end used by the end user in VR, and its hardware requirements are the focus of resource optimization for the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware resources.
Binary representation is a representation of zeros and ones that computers understand, unlike realistic representations perceived by humans.

A generic graphics system is a system with a host computer and a display, with a display controller, video memory, and a video controller between them; the CPU sends display commands to and may receive interaction data from the display controller, and the CPU passes rendering tasks to the display controller for execution in its GPU.

Video memory is the dedicated part of a computer's overall memory hierarchy, typically part of a separate graphics unit, that stores a digital image generated by a display controller for a video controller to render on a screen.

A video controller is a component of a generic graphics system that uses data stored in video memory to render an image on the display by converting the digital image into analog voltages that activate the pixels.
A graphic device is a device that is broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan and raster scan devices.

A vector scan device is a graphic device that views an image as continuous geometric primitives, such as lines and curves, and renders it by exciting only selected pixels, requiring high precision and making it costly and typically used in specialized settings.
A geometric primitive is a continuous part, such as a line or curve, that vector scan devices view an image as composed of.

A raster scan device is a graphic device that views an image as a whole pixel grid and activates all its pixels in sequence, typically left to right and top to bottom, using a frame buffer that stores each pixel's intensity.
Scanning is the sequential activation of all pixels in a pixel grid, typically left to right and top to bottom, with inputs that make the pixels emit light at appropriate intensities.
Raster scan rendering is a type of rendering in which pixels are excited in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order.

Frame buffer is a video memory component of a raster scan system that contains one memory location for each pixel, stores the pixel's intensity as a bit string, and has a size equal to the screen resolution.
A memory location is a part of a frame buffer that stores the intensity value for one pixel as a bit string of 0s and 1s.
Screen resolution is the size of a screen in a raster scan device.

A light-emitting element is a part of a display pixel that emits light; in color displays, each pixel typically contains three such elements that emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities.
Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels on a raster scan device, done to avoid fading and distortion and to keep the rendered image uniform even when the image is not changing.
Refresh rate is the number of times a scene is refreshed per second on a screen, represented in hertz.

Color display is a display in which each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three that emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities, sometimes four, and the eye perceives color from their mixed light.
Lighting is a stage of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that assigns color to a constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

Rasterization is the fifth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms continuous device coordinate descriptions into discrete pixel-grid screen descriptions by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.
Object representation is the first stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that defines the objects that form the rendered image in each object's local coordinate system.
A display processor is part of the display controller that computes the color values stored in the frame buffer in distinct stages.
Graphics pipeline is the set of distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.
A local coordinate system is an object's own coordinate system in the 3D graphics pipeline, in which objects are defined before modeling transformation transforms them to the world coordinate system.

Modeling transformation is the second stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that transforms an object’s local coordinate description into the common world coordinate system so that objects can be assembled into a scene.
The world coordinate system is the common reference frame in which all scene points are defined and to which objects are transformed from local coordinate systems to construct the scene.

The device coordinate system is a continuous two-dimensional coordinate system used to define the viewport, equivalent to but not the same as the screen, into which window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system, and whose real-number coordinates are converted by scan conversion into a discrete pixel-grid description.

The viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that selects a portion of a 3D scene and transforms it from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system through viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

Viewing transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that defines the view coordinate system and maps a scene from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional view coordinate system.

Projection transformation is a sub-stage of the viewing pipeline in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that maps objects from a three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional view plane or coordinate system.

Window-to-viewport transformation is a transformation in the viewing pipeline that maps a point from an abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, transforming the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

A screen coordinate system is one of the coordinate systems in a 3D graphics pipeline, the discrete pixel-grid coordinate system produced by scan conversion, in which each pixel coordinate is an integer.

Three-dimensional object representation is a representation of objects in a synthesized environment that balances realistic rendering of their shape, size, and intricate detail with the space and time efficiency of the subsequent stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline.

Point sample rendering is the simplest broad category of three-dimensional object representation techniques, in which scene information is captured from the real world as raw data points on the scene, each carrying attributes, and the points are processed or mapped to pixels to generate a synthetic image, relying on real-world information rather than synthetically defining objects.

Boundary representation is a broad category of three-dimensional object representation techniques in which objects are represented by the surfaces that define their boundary, with those surfaces being polygonal or curved. It comprises mesh, parametric, and implicit forms, with mesh as the most basic form.

Space partitioning based representation is a broad category of 3D object representation in which the space occupied by an object is divided into disjoint, non-overlapping regions, so any point inside the object lies in exactly one region and the object is represented by the occupied regions.

Mesh is a basic boundary representation technique in computer graphics that represents a three-dimensional object's surface as connected polygons, usually triangles, and stores the vertices and connections needed to reconstruct it.
A data point is a raw point in a scene that carries captured scene information as attributes in point sample rendering.
A vertex list is a list in mesh representation that stores all vertices and their connections.
An edge list is a list in a mesh representation that stores all edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curves and curved surfaces, falling under parametric representation, that represents complex shapes that simple polygons or simple polynomial equations cannot represent by several smoothly joined lower-degree polynomial pieces, each a basis or blending function, instead of one complex polynomial.
Polynomial representation is a representation of a curve by a polynomial, in which more complex curves are represented by higher-degree polynomials.

A polynomial piece is one of several lower-degree polynomials that make up a complete curve in spline representation; it computes points on the curve segment it represents, and the pieces must join smoothly and satisfy certain geometric and other properties.
A curve segment is a portion of a complete curve in spline representation that is represented by one lower-degree polynomial piece, called a blending or basis function.
A space partitioning tree is a hierarchical, tree-like structure that represents the space occupied by an object and is used to create a space partitioning representation.
Fractal representation is a specialized representation method for self-repeating structures.
Particle system representation is a specialized representation method for objects such as a waterfall that relies on the simulation of physical properties.

A skeletal model is a specialized representation method for complex characters that captures their overall appearance and motion behavior, typically used in animation or computer animation to represent objects or complex characters.
Rotation is a basic modeling transformation specified by a clockwise or anticlockwise angle around an axis.
A light source is an element that emits light that falls on a surface point directly or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces.

A lighting model is a computer graphics model used in color computation that simulates the reflection of incident light from a surface point to the viewer's eye, computing the intensity of that reflected light, which is the point's color, as a continuous value, typically between 0 and 1, mapped to discrete display values.

Light intensity is the strength of light reaching a point or the viewer’s eye, which determines the perceived color of a surface point; in the simple lighting model it is the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities and typically diminishes with distance from the light source.

A primary color is one of the red, green, and blue colors emitted by color display pixels, and in a colored light source model each has a corresponding intensity component whose combination gives the perception of any color.
Pixel intensity is the value between 0 and 1 that a lighting model computes for a pixel, which is mapped to a device-supported intensity whose bit pattern is stored in a frame buffer.

An object coordinate system is an individual coordinate system local to an object in which that object's position and dimension are defined, and from which a modeling transformation places it in a common scene or world coordinate system.

Translation is a basic transformation in modeling transformation, and in 2D it moves an object by translation amounts Tx and Ty along the x and y directions and is represented by a 3 by 3 matrix in the homogeneous coordinate system.

Scaling is a basic geometric transformation that increases or reduces an object's size using scaling factors along coordinate directions, and can be combined with other basic transformations to construct a scene.

Shearing is a basic modeling transformation that changes an object's shape. In 2D homogeneous coordinates, it can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix using shearing factors along the x and y directions.

A homogeneous coordinate system is a coordinate system in which one extra dimension is added so that a two-dimensional transformation can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix and a three-dimensional transformation by a 4 by 4 matrix.

A transformation matrix is a matrix that, when multiplied by a point vector, transforms the point from one coordinate system to another and is multiplied into a composite transformation matrix in right-to-left order of application.

A composite transformation matrix is a transformation matrix formed by multiplying individual transformation matrices, arranged right to left in the order the transformations are applied, to transform vertices or points when multiple basic transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing, are required.
A scaling matrix is a matrix that has Sx, the scaling factor along the x direction, and Sy, the scaling factor along the y direction.
The x-direction scaling factor is the scaling factor along the x direction in a scaling matrix.
Y-direction scaling factor is the scaling factor along the y direction in a scaling matrix.

A translation matrix is a matrix with Tx and Ty, the translations along the x-axis and y-axis, and, when translation is applied after scaling, it is placed to the left of the scaling matrix and multiplied to obtain the composite transformation matrix.
Translation along the x-axis is the value in a translation matrix used to move an object along the x-axis.
Translation along the y-axis is a value in a translation matrix that gives the movement of a vertex along the y-axis.

The order of application is the sequence in which individual transformations are applied, determining the placement of the transformation matrices in a composite transformation matrix: the first-applied matrix is rightmost and each later matrix is placed to the left. Because matrix multiplication is not commutative, an incorrect sequence may produce an incorrect transformed result.
A transformed vertex is a vertex in a world coordinate scene that is obtained by multiplying a current vertex by a transformation matrix.
Color computation is the third stage of the computer graphics pipeline that uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in a scene.

A shading model is an approximation of the color-assignment methods used by lighting models, which it relies on to assign colors to objects in the computer graphics pipeline while reducing computation without compromising the quality of experience.

A continuous intensity value is essentially a real number, typically within the range 0 to 1 and typically normalized, that lighting models use to compute colors and that is mapped to a discrete value.
Reflected light is light incident on a surface point and reflected to a viewer's eye, with its intensity determining the surface point's perceived color.

Simple lighting model is a lighting model that models the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point as the sum of ambient light intensity and the diffuse and specular reflection intensities of direct light.

Diffuse reflection component is direct light reflected in a diffuse manner from a surface in a simple lighting model, computed from the diffuse coefficient, source intensity, and the dot product of surface normal and light source direction, or zero when that dot product is not positive.
Specular reflection component is light in a simple lighting model that comes from a light source and is reflected with a specular effect, producing a shiny bright spot.

Reflected light intensity is the intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye, a fraction of the incident light intensity determined by the surface's reflection coefficient.

A reflection coefficient is a surface property that determines the fraction of incident light intensity reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye. In the simple lighting model, the ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients range from 0.0 to 1.0, where values near 0.0 are dull and values near 1.0 are shiny.
The specular component is the part of a simple lighting model that is computed for direct light with the Phong approximate model as Ks Is (V·r)^Ns, or 0 when V·r is not greater than 0.

Ambient reflection coefficient (Ka) is a reflection coefficient in a simple lighting model for ambient light, used to compute the ambient component of reflected light intensity by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on a surface point by Ka.
Diffuse reflection coefficient is a reflection coefficient in a simple lighting model for diffuse reflection of direct light, used to compute the diffuse reflection component.
Specular reflection coefficient is a reflection coefficient in a simple lighting model that is used for specular reflection of direct light.
The ambient component is the component of reflected light intensity computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on a surface point by the reflection coefficient for ambient light.
The Phong model is an approximate model used to compute the specular component.

Specular angle is the angle in the specular calculation between the viewer direction vector and the ideal specular reflection direction vector, the direction a mirror would reflect the light, and its cosine is the dot product of the two vectors.

The ideal specular reflection direction vector is the direction a mirror would reflect light, equal to twice the dot product of the light source direction vector and the surface normal vector times the surface normal vector, minus the light source direction vector.

Radial intensity attenuation factor is a lighting factor that accounts for the decrease in light intensity with distance from a light source to a surface point, typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of that distance using coefficients a0, a1, and a2, that can be varied for a more realistic effect.

Angular intensity attenuation is an attenuation factor in a simple lighting model, used primarily to generate spotlight effects by making elements outside the spotlight region darker and by multiplying the sum of the diffuse and specular reflection components, together with radial attenuation, while leaving the I_M intensity component unchanged.
A spotlight effect is an effect in which elements inside the spotlight region are visible or brightly visible and elements outside the spotlight zone are darker.
Spotlight region is the angular range in a spotlight effect, defined by theta, in which elements are visible or brightly visible and outside which they are darker.

An angular intensity attenuation factor is a factor in a lighting model that, in its commonly used form, multiplies the sum of the diffuse and specular reflection components by zero for a surface point outside the angular limit of a spotlight cone and by the cosine of phi to a positive angular attenuation exponent inside it.
Angular limit is the range of the spotlight cone, outside of which a surface point's angular intensity attenuation factor is zero.

An angular attenuation exponent (A1) is a positive exponent used in a spotlight's angular intensity attenuation factor, specifically the power to which the cosine of phi is raised for a surface point within the spotlight cone's angular limit.

A colored light source model is a model in which emitted light intensity is a three-element red, green, and blue vector rather than a single component, and its components are computed individually and combined to give the perception of any color.
Source intensity is a three-element vector in a colored light source model, with individual red, green, and blue components whose combination gives the perception of any color.

Intensity mapping is the mapping in which a lighting-model pixel intensity, which can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, is mapped to the nearest finite device-supported table intensity, so the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer.
An 8-bit display is a display that supports 256 intensity values per pixel.

Device-supported intensity value is one of the finite intensity levels supported by a display, determined from minimum and maximum values by successive multiplication by a factor r, because humans perceive relative changes, and used to map lighting-model pixel intensities to frame-buffer bit patterns.
Minimum device-supported intensity value is the minimum of the device-supported intensity values, measured with a photometer and used to determine the successive device-supported intensity values.

Multiplicative factor is a factor used to calculate successive device-supported intensity values from an initial intensity, based on human perception of relative rather than absolute intensity changes.
Psychophysiological property is a property that humans perceive relative changes between two intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity values.
Relative change is a change between two intensity values, rather than an absolute change in intensity values, that humans perceive.

A table is a store that holds calculated device-supported intensity values and their assigned bit patterns, used to map a lighting-model pixel intensity to the nearest stored intensity and the corresponding bit pattern.
Viewpoint is the user's field of view in a virtual world, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system, and it changes as the user moves from one point to another.

A view plane is the two-dimensional plane in a three-dimensional view coordinate system onto which a selected portion of a three-dimensional scene is projected; it is usually a rectangular area and an abstract intermediate representation that has nothing to do with the display.

Hidden surface removal is a GPU pixel-processing activity that identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from the viewer because they are occluded, using a depth buffer algorithm before rendering, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

Three-dimensional view coordinate system is a coordinate system that is defined from camera position, view-up point, and center of interest by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors and represents a scene after viewing transformation for clipping, hidden surface removal, and projection.

Three-dimensional viewing transformation is a transformation from 3D world coordinates to 3D view coordinates that simulates looking at a scene with a camera. After a view coordinate system is defined from camera parameters, it is performed by translation and rotation using a composite transformation matrix.
Camera parameters are the camera position, view-up point, and center of interest, also called the look-at point, used to set up the view coordinate system for a 3D viewing transformation.
Origin vector is a vector representing the camera position in the world coordinate system and one of the camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system.
View-up point is a camera parameter, represented as a vector, whose vector from the camera origin gives the view-up direction used to set up a view coordinate system.
Center of interest is a camera parameter that, with the camera position, determines the looking direction used to set up the view coordinate system.
A unit basis vector is one of three mutually orthogonal vectors that define a view coordinate system.

A view volume is a three-dimensional region in the scene that defines the portion of the scene projected onto the view plane; objects inside it are projected, and objects outside it are discarded. For parallel projection it is a rectangular parallelepiped, and for perspective projection a frustum, with one face or side serving as the clipping window.

Perspective projection is a projection type in which projectors from an object in a three-dimensional view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel but converge at a center of projection; the view volume is a frustum, and realistic rendering is produced for realistic scenes.

A center of projection is the point where projectors from an object in the 3D view coordinate system to the view plane converge in perspective projection, or the point at infinity in parallel projection.
Parallel projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object to the view plane are parallel to each other, so their center of projection is at infinity and they never meet.
A frustum is the view volume for perspective projection, with one face or side serving as the clipping window on which objects inside it are projected.

The naive clipping method is a method that computes the intersection of view volume boundaries with object boundaries, a calculation that is computationally intensive for arbitrarily shaped view volumes such as frustums.
Canonical view volume is a normalized cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted to simplify pipeline computations.

A parallel projection matrix is a four-by-four matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin, that is used to compute a parallel projection by multiplying a point vector in the 3D view coordinate system and dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by w, typically not 1, to obtain Cartesian x, y, and z values.
The homogeneous factor is a factor, typically not equal to 1, by which obtained homogeneous coordinate values are divided to obtain Cartesian coordinates in parallel and perspective projection.

A perspective projection matrix is a matrix used to compute a perspective projection by multiplying a point vector in the 3D view coordinate system, where D is the distance from the clipping window to the center of projection, typically assumed at the origin; the obtained homogeneous coordinate values are then divided by the homogeneous factor w.
A viewport is a portion of the final screen in device space, not on the view plane, where a scene is rendered, defined relative to the display origin and dimensions in a continuous coordinate system.
A window point is a point in the abstract window representation, given as (Wx, Wy), that is mapped by the window-to-viewport transformation to a viewport point.
Viewport point is a point in a device-specific viewport representation, mapped from an abstract window point by the window-to-viewport transformation.

The window-to-viewport transformation matrix is a three-by-three matrix whose Sx and Sy are defined in terms of window and viewport dimensions, and whose Tx and Ty are computed from Sx, Sy, and those dimensions. Multiplying a window point vector by the matrix yields a homogeneous coordinate representation, whose Cartesian point is obtained by dividing by the homogeneous factor W.
A cartesian point is a point obtained by dividing a point in homogeneous coordinate representation by the homogeneous factor W.

A triangular mesh is a three-dimensional surface made of triangles, into which graphics systems convert surfaces for a scene to be rendered regardless of how a developer defines an object, and whose vertices a GPU receives as input, one at a time, to assemble into triangles.

Application programming interface (API) is a predefined set of functions provided by a library that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks, allowing a programmer to deal with lower-level tasks without needing to know every detail of the underlying system or platform.

A native rendering library is a software library that sits above an operating system and provides graphics APIs that a virtual reality or game engine calls to perform rendering, rather than the developer accessing it directly.
Pixel grid is a discrete coordinate system of pixels that a display device uses to render an image, and its points can only have integer coordinates.
Depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel in a two-dimensional projection of a three-dimensional scene.

View pipeline is the part of the 3D graphics pipeline after the viewing transformation that includes clipping and hidden surface removal in the 3D view coordinate system, projection transformation from the 3D view coordinate system to the 2D view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the 2D view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.
A continuous coordinate system is a coordinate system whose coordinate values can be any real number.

A mapping algorithm is an algorithm used in scan conversion that transforms continuous two-dimensional viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.

Viewport coordinates are the continuous two-dimensional coordinate values in the device coordinate system used to define a viewport, mapped to discrete pixel-grid coordinates by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels during scan conversion.

Pixel-grid coordinate system is a discrete coordinate system into which scan conversion transforms continuous two-dimensional viewport coordinates by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a line is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

Point rendering is a rounding method that maps a point with real-number coordinates in device space to the nearest integer coordinate values in discrete space, suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines or circles.

Rounding is a method in point rendering that maps real-number coordinates to the nearest integer coordinate values, moving a point from device space to discrete space, and is suitable for points, not for other geometric shapes.
Line rendering is a method for drawing a line by identifying the pixels that approximately represent it, and efficient methods use integer arithmetic to avoid floating-point operations.
A line-rendering algorithm is an algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line, and efficient versions aim to avoid floating-point operations.

Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels approximating a line segment from its endpoints while using integer arithmetic and avoiding floating-point operations.
Delta x is the difference between the x coordinates of two line endpoints, computed in Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm.
Delta y is the difference between the y coordinates of the two endpoints in Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm.

Decision parameter is a value in a line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1 that is computed as twice delta y minus delta x and used to decide whether the next pixel increments x only or both x and y.
